Tomatoes. Bread. Coffee. Call landlord.

At the bottom, beneath a line drawn in blue ink, Daniel had written: *Marry me?*

Mara sat down.

“You said yes on the back.”

She turned it over, although she remembered now. Their first apartment. Rain at the kitchen window. Daniel standing beside the refrigerator, trying to seem casual while she put away groceries.

*Yes. But we still need coffee.*

She laughed, then pressed the paper flat with her palm.

“I thought you’d thrown it away.”

“I thought about framing it, but then nobody would ever ask us to be serious adults again.”

“They’ve already stopped.”

He sat opposite her. For a moment neither reached for a fork.

Then Mara tasted the pasta.

“Cold,” she said.

“I know.”

“Very good, though.”

She took another bite. “I know that, too.”

They ate slowly. Daniel told the story of getting lost on their honeymoon, and Mara corrected the parts he always improved. She reminded him of the restaurant where he had confidently ordered six bowls of soup. He insisted that some of the best travel involved misunderstandings.

When he reached for the wine, his sleeve caught a rose petal and carried it halfway across the table. Mara picked it off his cuff.

Such a small gesture. Yet he went quiet beneath it.

“What?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

“Daniel.”

He glanced at her hand, still resting near his wrist.

They had been in the same house all week. They had discussed a leaking tap, answered messages over breakfast, fallen asleep on opposite edges of exhaustion.

Mara turned her hand over.

He took it.

He smiled, but his voice was gentle when he said, “Would you marry me?”

She pretended to consider.

Mara touched his cheek.

He kissed her, softly at first. She caught the front of his shirt when he started to draw back.

“Yes,” she said again, before he could ask anything.

The stranger wore a silver mask and no ornament except a black ribbon at his throat.

“You’ve been watching the doors,” he said.

Clara turned from the ballroom windows. “Perhaps I’m waiting for someone.”

“Are you?”

She glanced toward the entrance, where another laughing couple had just arrived. “Not anymore.”

He offered his hand. “Then would you like to dance?”

It was a better invitation than the ones she’d received all evening. No elaborate compliment, no assumption that she ought to be grateful. She set her glass on a passing tray and took his hand.

On the dance floor, he let her find the rhythm before drawing her closer. His mask concealed his expression, but not the amusement at the corners of his mouth when she corrected his step.

“You noticed.”

“You hoped I wouldn’t?”

“I hoped you’d be kind.”

“I haven’t decided yet.”

By the second dance, she had stopped looking at the doors.

Later, they escaped into a corridor lined with portraits and found a small sitting room open to the terrace. The music followed them faintly through the walls. Clara stood beside the unlit fireplace while he remained near the doorway.

“Should I go?” he asked.

“No.”

He came closer, slowly enough that the last step was hers.

Their first kiss was tentative. The second was not. Clara caught his lapels and laughed softly when his mask knocked against hers.

“These are becoming inconvenient,” she said.

He reached for his ribbon, then paused. “You first?”

“Together.”

Without the mask, he looked less mysterious and more nervous. She liked him better for it.

“I’m Daniel,” he said.

“Clara.”

“Hello, Clara.”

She kissed him again.

When he drew back, she touched his cheek, keeping him close. Beyond the terrace doors, the garden lanterns trembled in the wind; somewhere in the ballroom, a new waltz began.

“We could still go back,” he murmured.

Clara considered the crowded floor, her abandoned glass, the evening she had expected to endure.

Then she crossed to the sitting-room door and closed it.

When they returned, the orchestra was packing away its music.

Clara carried her mask. Daniel’s ribbon hung loose at his collar.

At the foot of the staircase, he asked whether he might see her again.

“In daylight?” she said.

“If you’d like.”

She took his offered arm. “I think I would.”

None of that had prepared her for his weight leaning into hers.

“I thought so too.”

“I know. You showed me.”

“I was being an idiot.”

She took his hand and led him down the hall.

Later, they lay beneath the tangled duvet while rain ticked against the window. His suitcase was still in the entrance hall. Neither of them had eaten.

“I had a whole speech planned for the station,” she murmured.

“Was it good?”

“Extremely.”

“Let’s hear it.”

She rolled toward him. He lifted the covers so she could settle closer, an old habit resumed without discussion.

Then she put her hand against his cheek.

“Welcome home,” she said.

“I panicked. Normally I’m much more mysterious.”

“Try again.”

“That’s better.”

You glance at their hand resting on the bar. “Are you always this direct?”

“No. Usually I go home and think of something clever to say.”

“And tonight?”

“You sat down.”

You laugh, and Alex looks pleased—not triumphant, just pleased.

Conversation carries you through one drink. You learn that Alex hates their hotel’s pillows, likes old movies without pretending to have seen all of them, and has been trying not to check your mouth every time you speak.

“You’re doing it again,” you say.

“I know.”

“Not very subtle.”

“I could look at the cocktail menu instead, but I’ve already made my choice.”

“Was that a line?”

“A bad one. Give me a minute to recover.”

You lean closer. “What if I don’t?”

For the first time, Alex loses the answer.

“Oh,” you say. “There you are.”

“Where?”

“Underneath all that confidence.”

Alex’s smile softens. “You make me a little nervous.”

“Good nervous?”

“Very.”

Outside, the night air is cool enough to bring you shoulder to shoulder beneath the awning.

“My hotel’s across the street,” Alex says. “You could come up. We could keep talking somewhere I don’t have to compete with a terrible saxophone solo.”

“That solo really upset you.”

“It had no ending.”

“And what would we talk about upstairs?”

Alex meets your eyes. “Whether I can kiss you.”

“You could ask me that here.”

“Can I kiss you?”

“Yes.”

The kiss is brief, almost careful. When you draw back, Alex stays close without following.

“Well?” they ask.

“You’re quieter than I expected.”

“I’m revising my whole approach.”

“Don’t,” they say.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re thinking loudly.”

“I like knowing you’re not entirely composed.”

The lock flashes green.

Inside, a lamp throws warm light across a chair, an untouched bed, a suitcase that has lost an argument with its owner.

“You weren’t expecting company,” you say.

“No. Give me ten seconds to become the sort of person who puts clothes away.”

You catch their hand before they can reach the suitcase.

“Leave it.”

Alex turns back toward you.

“Still okay?” they ask.

“Yes. You?”

“Yes.”

“Then stop looking like you’re waiting for a performance review.”

A laugh escapes them. “You’re a little bossy.”

“Only when someone needs help.”

“And do I?”

“You tell me.”

Alex steps closer. “I’d like another kiss.”

“That sounded almost shy.”

“It wasn’t meant to.”

“I liked it.”

This time you meet halfway. Their hand settles at your waist; yours finds the collar of their shirt. Beyond the window, a horn sounds and fades into traffic.

When you separate, Alex rests their forehead lightly against yours.

“I had several clever things planned,” they murmur.

“Save them.”

“For when?”

“Breakfast.”

Alex pulls back enough to see your face. “That an invitation?”

“A possibility.”

“I can work with a possibility.”

You kiss them before they can improve the line.

Later, when Alex reaches for the lamp, they pause.

“On or off?”

“Off.”

The switch clicks, and the conversation grows quiet.

You recognize the knock before you open the door: two quick taps, a pause, then one more. For a year, you have imagined this moment with impossible precision. Now you can barely manage the latch.

Your lover stands in the corridor, rain darkening the shoulders of their coat.

“Hello,” they say, and the smallness of it breaks your heart a little.

You reach for their hand.

Their fingers are cold. That surprises you—the ordinary fact of it, after so many months of loving a voice through a speaker. You draw them inside and hold their hand between both of yours while the door swings shut.

For a moment, neither of you moves.

Then their palm settles against your cheek.

You close your eyes. There it is: the familiar breadth of their hand, the rough place near the thumb, the warmth arriving slowly beneath rain-chilled skin. You turn your face into their touch.

“I missed this,” you whisper.

They kiss your forehead first, almost cautiously. Your cheek next. When their mouth finally meets yours, the kiss is brief enough to leave you both staring afterward, smiling with a kind of disbelief.

“Again,” you say.

This time, you have the courage to pull them closer.

Outside, tires hiss along the wet boulevard. Somewhere below the window, a waiter stacks café chairs with a metallic clatter. You hear these things with startling clarity, along with the rustle of your lover’s coat as it slips from their shoulders and lands badly on the chair.

You laugh against their mouth.

“What?”

“Nothing. You’re here.”

“I’m here.”

You had planned champagne. There is a bottle waiting in a silver bucket, two glasses beside it, and neither of you remembers it until much later.

Instead, you sit together on the edge of the bed, knees touching, still holding hands. Lamplight catches the faint new lines beside their eyes. You trace one with a fingertip.

For months, you had saved stories for this meeting. Now they come back in fragments: a disastrous dinner, a missed train, something your neighbor said. Your lover laughs, and you feel it where their shoulder rests against yours.

Then conversation falters.

“You look tired,” they say.

“I didn’t sleep much last night.”

“Neither did I.”

Their arm comes around you. You lean into them, and the breath you release seems to have been waiting all year. They hold you without trying to hurry the moment. When your eyes sting, you let them.

Later, you stand by the window while they loosen the clasp of your necklace. Their fingertips brush the back of your neck; you shiver at the cool air left behind when they lift the chain away.

“Still all right?” they ask softly.

You turn and kiss them in answer, then say it aloud. “Yes.”

The curtains close on the shining street.

In the quiet that follows, there is time to be shy, time to laugh, time to rediscover how easily tenderness can undo you. The lamplight goes out. Whatever you imagined while you were apart gives way to being here together, without a screen between you or a departure waiting in the morning.

Much later, you wake beneath the light weight of the linen sheet. Your lover is beside you, one hand resting loosely over yours. The room smells faintly of rain and the soap from the hotel bathroom.

“Water?” they murmur.

You nod. They reach for the glass on the bedside table and pass it to you, then wait while you drink.

When you settle back, they lift the sheet for you.

You fit yourself against their side. Their thumb moves once across your knuckles, then grows still.

Beyond the curtains, Paris is beginning its morning. You close your eyes again.

The bulb over the table had a brown stain inside it. A dead moth, maybe. Something that had mistaken light for a way out.

Detective Voss stood by the door smoking a cigarette down to the cork. Detective Harlan held the city directory in both hands.

“You fell down some stairs,” Harlan said.

“I haven’t yet.”

He hit me across the ribs with the phone book.

The chair skidded an inch. Something inside me tried to fold in half, but the cuffs behind my back wouldn’t let it. I sucked air through my teeth and got almost none.

Harlan waited until I could look at him.

“Now you have.”

Cheap tobacco hung in the room, thick and sour. Voss smoked the kind they sold beside aspirin and mouse traps. It had soaked into his coat, the curtains over the wired glass, probably the plaster. I concentrated on the smell. It was something to think about besides my ribs.

Voss tapped ash into a cold cup of coffee.

“Where’s the girl, Mercer?”

“Which girl?”

Harlan lifted the directory.

“The one worth learning all these telephone numbers for,” I said.

He struck me again, lower this time. I bent as far as the cuffs allowed. For a few seconds there was nothing in the world but the edge of the table and the need to breathe.

Harlan leaned close. His tie had a gravy spot on it.

“No bruises,” he said, patting the cover.

He sounded proud of that. I’d known men who were proud of worse.

Voss pulled out the chair opposite me and sat. He laid my private investigator’s license on the table, followed by my wallet and the photograph they’d taken from my office.

In the photograph, Evelyn Marsh stood beside a black Packard. She was smiling at someone outside the frame.

Voss put his cigarette on her face.

“You’ve got a modest business,” he said. “Divorces. Missing husbands. Insurance work. Nobody bothers you.”

“You broke my door.”

“We knocked.”

“With the janitor.”

“He was cooperative.”

Blood had collected where I’d bitten the inside of my cheek. I swallowed it. Bad idea. My stomach rolled, and Harlan watched with professional interest.

Voss slid the photograph toward me.

“She stole from people who can afford to be angry.”

“So arrest her.”

“We’re trying to find her.”

“No warrant. No booking sheet.” I looked toward the door. “You boys working on commission tonight?”

Harlan moved, but Voss raised a finger. Harlan stopped. That told me something I wished I’d learned before the first swing.

“You don’t have to like this,” Voss said. “Just give us an address.”

Outside, a telephone rang. A man laughed. Somewhere down the hall, somebody was asking for a lawyer with less and less conviction.

I looked at Evelyn’s photograph. The cigarette had burned a small black hole through her smile.

At six that evening she’d sat in my office holding a glass of water with both hands. She hadn’t touched it. When I asked who she was afraid of, she’d said, *The police*, and watched me carefully.

I’d thought she meant prison.

Voss crushed out his cigarette.

“Last chance.”

I tested a breath. It hurt all the way in.

“Then you ought to ask a better question.”

Voss stood and moved his coffee off the table.

Harlan opened the directory to the middle, flexed it, and closed it again.

I fixed my eyes on the dead moth in the bulb.

The closet smelled of cedar and the raincoat pressed against Mara’s face.

Downstairs, a drawer hit the floor.

She flinched before she could stop herself. The hangers above her gave a faint metallic tick.

Silence.

Mara held her breath. Through the slats, she could see a narrow strip of hallway: pale carpet, the leg of the console table, her husband’s running shoes where he’d kicked them off that morning.

He was still at work. She had checked the time when the glass broke.

He should still be at work.

“Now, where did you go?”

The voice came from the foot of the stairs. Conversational, almost weary.

Her phone lay on the kitchen counter. She pictured it beside the cutting board, its screen lighting up with a message she couldn’t answer. She had been slicing a lemon. The knife was there, too.

A stair creaked.

Then another.

“No car leaving,” the man said. “Back door’s still locked.”

Mara eased her hand over her mouth. Her wedding ring caught against her teeth.

At the top of the stairs, the footsteps stopped.

“Should’ve just stayed downstairs.”

Something brushed the wall. Through the slats, a shadow crossed the carpet, followed by a boot. The man passed the closet without looking at it.

In his right hand, held low beside his leg, was a pistol.

Mara shut her eyes. Opened them again.

The bedroom door bumped against its stopper.

She heard the bed frame shift. A sharp rattle as he pulled open the nightstand. He was not moving quickly. He had time to check under things.

“People always say they didn’t see your face,” he murmured. “Then they remember.”

A drawer slid shut.

“Can’t leave anyone to remember.”

Mara stared at the shoes in the hallway.

Her husband would come home and see the broken glass. Unless he came in through the garage. He always came in through the garage.

She pressed harder against her mouth.

The man entered the bathroom. The shower curtain scraped along its rail.

“Empty.”

He sounded annoyed now.

Mara’s left foot had gone numb beneath her. She tried to shift her weight, a fraction at a time, but the floorboard under her heel gave a small, dry pop.

The shower rings stopped rattling.

For several seconds, she heard nothing.

Then a boot appeared in the gap beneath the closet door.

Mara went still, one hand clamped over her mouth, the other braced against the floor. Dust clung to her damp palm.

On the far side of the door, the man breathed through his nose.

“There.”

The handle turned.

The closet door began to creak open.

The hotel had folded the end of the toilet paper into a triangle. Someone had signed a card beside the bed to certify that the room had been prepared with care.

He placed the card in a drawer.

On the desk, beneath the brass reading lamp, the rifle lay on a hotel towel. Receiver, bolt assembly, barrel, stock: objects with tolerances and replacement costs. There was a pale scratch on the trigger guard that he remembered from three contracts ago. He examined it, decided it had not worsened, and continued wiping the exterior metalwork.

The television was reporting a death.

“—pronounced at the scene,” the woman at the news desk said.

He looked up to confirm the photograph. Same face. Same slightly raised left eyebrow. The image had probably been taken for a company website; the dead man stood in front of glass offices with his hands arranged to suggest openness.

He returned his attention to the rifle.

The cloth had left a fiber near the receiver. He removed it with a fingernail.

According to the report, the deceased was a prominent developer, a philanthropist, and a father of two. These categories appeared in that order. A former colleague described him as indefatigable.

The man at the desk listened without revising anything.

His file had contained a name, photographs, and the terms under which payment became due. None of the information now being broadcast altered those terms. Fatherhood did not invalidate a contract. Philanthropy did not require an adjustment to the invoice.

He disliked the word *target* after completion. It described an ongoing relationship.

The news cut to footage of the man entering a building earlier that week. He held the door for someone behind him, then hurried out of frame.

The rifle’s stock bore a dull print from the heel of a hand. The cleaner supplied by the hotel had a citrus smell that competed with the solvent on his cloth. He would mention that in the room review only if he remembered. He generally did not leave reviews.

His phone vibrated.

**Confirmed.**

Below it, a second message:

**Balance released.**

He checked the amount. Correct.

There was a field in his ledger for expenses and another for variance. He entered the hotel charge, transport, meals. Under variance he wrote *none*. The word referred to the agreement, not the day. There had been minor inconveniences, but he saw no reason to bill for them.

On television, a reporter stood behind a barrier while people moved in the background. The reporter said the family had requested privacy. Then the broadcast showed the family’s front gate.

He reduced the volume.

He inspected the scope housing under the lamp. No damage. The bolt handle caught a narrow stripe of light; the muzzle rested beyond the edge of the towel. He turned the rifle slightly so no metal touched the desk.

The station returned to the photograph.

For a few seconds he studied the dead man’s expression. He had spent enough time examining that face that seeing it selected by strangers felt faintly administrative, as if another department had taken possession of the file.

He closed his ledger.

The hotel offered breakfast from six until ten. His train departed at eight forty. That allowed time to eat without rushing, provided the dining room opened promptly.

He put the rifle away and checked the desk for anything he might have missed.

At the door, he paused to hang out the breakfast order. Two eggs, toast, black coffee. The form asked for the number of guests.

He wrote **1**.

By midnight, the industrial district belonged to the engines.

They idled beneath the overpass in two trembling rows, headlights bleaching the concrete pillars. Money changed hands through open windows. Somewhere behind the crowd, a woman laughed too loudly, and someone shouted the size of the pot.

Thirty thousand dollars.

Mara kept both hands on the wheel.

Beside her, a silver coupe snapped its throttle. The sound punched through her door and settled in her ribs. She watched the starter step between them, one arm raised, his white sleeve bright against the dark.

Burning rubber drifted in through her window. Beneath it came the raw stink of gasoline.

Her phone buzzed in the cup holder.

**Win, and we’re square.**

She turned it facedown.

The starter dropped his arm.

Mara launched.

For a second there was nothing but wheelspin and violence: the steering wheel twitching against her grip, the rear tires shrieking, smoke swallowing the people behind her. Then the tires caught. Her head struck the seat. The crowd vanished.

Second gear.

The coupe stayed level, its driver a pale blur beyond the glass.

Third.

Warehouses whipped past in long corrugated streaks. At the first bend, Mara eased off, turned in, and felt the car settle onto its outside tires. The coupe drifted wide. She came out ahead.

A laugh escaped her before she could stop it.

She had this.

The final straight opened between chain-link fences. At its far end, amber work lights marked the intersection where the course hooked left around a construction site. Beyond the turn stood a concrete barrier.

Mara checked the mirror. Two car lengths.

She waited for the mark she’d chosen during the walk-through: a loading-bay door with a white diagonal stripe. It flashed into her headlights.

She pressed the brake.

The pedal sank beneath her foot without resistance.

For an instant she simply held it there, waiting for the car to slow.

It didn’t.

She lifted and pressed again. The pedal hit the floor.

“No.”

The barrier grew wider in the windshield.

She pumped the brake, fast and hard. Nothing. Her knee struck the underside of the steering column. The engine still roared, absurdly loud, though she had taken her foot off the accelerator.

A memory surfaced with sickening clarity: a man crouched beside her front wheel before the race. She had asked what he was doing.

*Checking something for you.*

He’d stood, wiped his fingers on a rag, and smiled.

They hadn’t expected her to win.

Mara screamed, “Get out of the way!” at the spectators waiting near the turn.

A few looked up. One kept filming.

She hit the horn and held it.

The silver coupe flashed past on her right, already braking, its red taillights blazing. Mara hauled at the gearshift. The engine shrieked. The car lurched, slowing a little, nowhere near enough.

Now the people ran.

A folding chair toppled into the road. Someone fell against the fence and scrambled upright. The phone disappeared from the spectator’s hand.

Mara turned toward the narrow opening beside the barrier.

For half a heartbeat, she thought she could fit.

Then the rear of the car swung out.

The headlights swept across wire fencing, a yellow excavator, faces twisted away. Her hands worked uselessly at the wheel. She saw the barrier through the side of the windshield and pulled her chin down.

The impact tore the sound out of the world.

Steel buckled with a deep, crushing bang. Her body drove forward into the belt; the airbag struck her face. Glass burst across the cabin in glittering sheets. The car spun off the concrete, scraping sparks along the road, and slammed backward into the fence.

Then it stopped.

Mara couldn’t breathe.

She clawed at the belt, mouth open, trying to draw air into a chest that refused to move. A thin electronic tone sounded somewhere near her knees. Dust from the airbag hung in the headlights, which now pointed in different directions.

Her first breath came shallow and agonizing.

Outside, someone shouted, “Fuel!”

She smelled it immediately: gasoline, sharp enough to taste. Hot rubber. Burned wiring.

Mara fumbled for the buckle. Her fingers kept sliding off it.

Orange light flickered beyond the broken hood.

“No, no, come on—”

The belt released. She dropped sideways against the door and screamed at the pain in her shoulder. The handle moved, but the door stayed shut.

A face appeared at the shattered window.

“Cover your eyes!”

Hands reached through. Metal scraped. Someone pulled at her jacket while another voice shouted behind him. Mara tried to help, pushing with her legs, but one foot was trapped beneath the pedals.

Then it came free.

They dragged her through the window and across the asphalt. Gravel rasped her back. She could hear the fire now, a low rushing sound beneath the shouting.

When they stopped pulling, she rolled onto her side.

Her car burned against the fence. Flames climbed out of the engine bay and curled over the roof, lighting the underside of the overpass. People stood at a distance, phones raised again.

Across the road, among the retreating spectators, Mara saw the man with the rag.

He watched until he realized she was looking at him.

Then he turned and walked away.

The basement light was already on.

That was what stopped Mara halfway down the stairs. She remembered shutting it off that afternoon, remembered the stubborn pull-chain and the bulb swinging above the laundry sink.

Now it hung perfectly still.

“Jess?”

The furnace clicked. Somewhere beyond it, water dripped into a shallow pool.

Mara descended another step. The wooden tread bent beneath her shoe.

She found Ben first.

He sat against the washing machine, his chin lowered as if he’d fallen asleep waiting for a load to finish. One hand rested palm-up beside him. His ridiculous yellow watch was still blinking.

Mara waited for him to lift his head.

“Ben. Come on.”

Her voice sounded small among the pipes and concrete.

She reached the floor and crouched beside him. His sleeve was damp. When she touched his wrist, its coldness made her let go.

“No.”

She said it again, louder, as if he had misunderstood.

A shoe lay near the workbench. White canvas, green laces. Jess had drawn little stars along its rubber sole during the drive up.

Mara followed the green lace with her eyes.

Jess lay beyond the bench, partly hidden beneath a fallen sheet of plastic. One bare foot showed. The plastic whispered in the draft from the furnace, rising and settling just enough to make Mara take a hopeful step.

Then the furnace stopped.

The plastic went still.

Across the room, beneath the narrow window, someone had pulled a blue moving blanket over another figure. Eric’s glasses sat folded on top. He never folded them. He dropped them on tables, left them open on the bathroom sink, fell asleep wearing them.

Mara stared at those neatly crossed arms of black plastic.

There were three of them down here.

She had been upstairs calling their phones.

A faint electronic buzz came from Ben’s pocket. Mara flinched so hard her shoulder struck the washing machine.

His phone lit through the fabric.

She already knew what the screen would say: her name, the photograph he’d taken of her asleep in the passenger seat, mouth open.

The buzzing stopped.

Mara backed toward the stairs. Her heel caught the white shoe and pushed it across the floor with a soft rubber squeak. She bent to put it back without knowing why, then froze with her hand extended.

Above her, a floorboard creaked.

She looked at the ceiling.

Another creak. Slow. Directly overhead.

Her phone was in her jacket pocket. She eased it out, shielding the screen against her stomach. No signal.

At the top of the stairs, the door began to open.

Mara slipped behind the furnace and pressed both hands over her mouth.

Light spread down the steps. She could see Ben through the gap between two pipes, his yellow watch blinking steadily.

A shoe touched the first stair.

Then a voice said, quite gently, “Mara?”

She shut her eyes.

It was the voice that had told her to check the basement.

The airlock failed with a metallic crack.

Air hurled Mara against the outer hatch, carrying her shout away before it became a word. She reached for the emergency lever. Her fingers struck it once, slipped, and reached again.

There was no breath to take.

A bubbling sensation troubled the wet surface of her tongue. She thought, with sudden, absolute terror: *My blood is boiling.*

It wasn’t—not inside the shelter of her veins. But the moisture in her mouth was beginning to vaporize in the falling pressure. Her eyes stung as their thin film of tears evaporated. She tried to blink the pain away, still staring at the yellow lever just beyond her hand.

The edges of it darkened.

She had trained for this. There was something she was supposed to do, something simple. Her hand remained outstretched while the thought dissolved.

Within seconds, she lost consciousness. Her arm drifted down without quite coming to rest.

Death followed from the lack of oxygen, not the cold. For a little while, her body retained its warmth in the empty chamber. The freezing came later, slowly, without the mercy or violence she had imagined.

By then, tiny crystals had gathered along her lashes. Frost clouded the exposed moisture of her eyes, softening the fixed reflection of the emergency light.

The lever remained yellow. The light continued to flash.

Beyond the hatch, the stars did not flicker.

The prison had no bars. It had excellent windows, a garden on every floor, and doors that opened when you approached them.

Beyond the doors were more rooms.

Every morning, a voice came from the ceiling.

“Are you ready to understand?”

For the first eleven days, Tomas said no.

On the twelfth, he asked whether it mattered.

“No,” the voice said. “But we are required to ask.”

***

The woman he had killed was called Elian Voss.

At his trial, Tomas had learned her age, occupation, and the names of the people who survived her. None of it had stayed with him. He remembered the faulty microphone better: the prosecutor tapping its head, the sudden bark of feedback.

In the rehabilitation chair, they gave him something he could not mishear.

A technician fitted a silver mesh over his scalp. She tightened one contact, checked a display, then loosened it again.

“The reconstruction incorporates neural residue, sensory records, and corroborating personal data,” she said. “You may notice discontinuities.”

“Is it really her?”

“It is the closest available experience.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

She placed a rubber switch in his hand.

“What’s this?”

“You can use it to report distress.”

“Does it stop?”

She looked at him then.

“No.”

***

First, there was a tooth.

A dull ache in the back of her jaw. Elian had been postponing a dental appointment because the clinic was across town, and because it hurt only when she drank something cold.

Tomas had not expected this.

He had expected the street, the weapon, himself.

Instead he stood at a kitchen counter, testing soup with a wooden spoon.

Rain ticked against the window. His left sock—or hers—had slipped halfway under the heel. There was a message waiting from her sister. Elian glanced at it, decided to answer after work, and put the phone facedown.

Tomas tried to turn back to it.

Her hand kept stirring.

He could feel everything and choose nothing.

Then came the street.

He recognized the blue pharmacy sign. The parked delivery van. His own reflection moving toward her in a dark shop window.

Inside the chair, somewhere very far away, his fingers closed around the switch.

Elian noticed him and did not become afraid immediately.

She moved aside to let him pass.

That small courtesy was worse than anything Tomas had prepared himself for.

He felt her attention lift toward his face. She was wondering whether he needed directions. Then she saw what he held, and her thoughts lost their easy sequence.

*Oh.*

A single astonished syllable.

Her body understood before she did. Her stomach tightened so violently it seemed to pull the rest of her inward. Her mouth dried. Sound grew strange: the traffic receded, while the rasp of his sleeve was terribly close.

She could not remember whether she had locked her apartment.

The thought arrived whole and useless, and she clung to it. A locked door belonged to a world with tomorrow in it.

Then she began looking for the correct thing to say.

Tomas felt the work of it—the desperate sorting of words, her effort to keep her voice gentle, to avoid startling him. She offered her bag. She explained that her hands were moving because she was getting the strap off her shoulder.

He remembered being irritated that she talked so much.

Now he lived inside every word she chose.

She was trying to get home.

When the violence came, the reconstruction blurred at its edges. There were gaps, bright interruptions, a confusion of pavement and sky.

The terror remained precise.

She could no longer get enough air. Each failed breath consumed all her attention, then left just enough for her to know another was needed. She wanted to call out, but first she had to breathe, and the breath would not come properly.

Her hand searched the pavement.

Tomas felt the grit beneath her fingertips, the absurd care with which she tried to find something to hold. There was nothing there but wet concrete.

She thought of her sister waiting for an answer.

Then she thought, with sudden relief, that someone would come. This was a street. People came down streets. She only had to stay where she was.

He felt that hope falter.

The crushing thing was how hard she kept trying. Even when she could no longer move her hand, some part of her was still preparing the next breath, still listening for footsteps, still refusing to understand that there might be no help.

Tomas tried to speak to her.

He was inside her fear, and could offer her nothing.

***

He woke making a thin, repetitive sound.

The technician removed the mesh. He could see a damp crescent where he had bitten his lip.

“How long?”

“Forty-three minutes.”

“No. At the end.”

“Seventy-six seconds.”

He stared at the switch in his hand.

“Did you hear me?”

“Yes,” she said.

***

After thirty sessions, Tomas could identify Elian’s sister by her footsteps. After fifty, he knew which cupboard held the chipped bowl she preferred and why she disliked the smell of lavender.

The prison called this progress.

He ate little. He slept with a light on. In the garden, he sat where he could see both doors.

At his quarterly review, a clinician showed him a graph. Several lines had risen sharply.

“Your empathic response is well above the release threshold.”

“Then you’re releasing me?”

“Other criteria remain.”

Tomas looked at a still image of Elian on the clinician’s screen. She was laughing at something outside the frame.

“Does her sister know what you do here?”

“She authorized the use of the reconstruction.”

“Has she seen it?”

“That isn’t part of your assessment.”

He asked again the next quarter.

Eventually, they allowed a call.

Her sister appeared against a kitchen wall Tomas recognized. He almost said, *You moved the table.*

Instead he kept his hands in his lap.

“They told me this would help you understand,” she said.

“I understand more than I did.”

“Good.”

He nodded.

She waited, weary and watchful. He realized she expected something from him: an apology, perhaps, or an account of his suffering. The prison had coached him in both.

“Would you tell me something about her?” he asked.

Her face tightened.

“You’ve had access to nearly everything.”

“Yes.”

For a while, neither spoke.

Then her sister said, “She was a terrible singer.”

Tomas knew that already. He had heard Elian singing at the kitchen counter, comfortably off-key.

He let her tell him.

I can describe the physical effects and equipment failure, but not graphic details of burned flesh.

If the person remains conscious, the initial current could cause an overwhelming shock, involuntary muscle contractions, and an inability to move or breathe normally. Sustained contractions may feel like severe cramping, while poor electrode contact can concentrate heat and cause painful burns. Electrical injury can also disrupt the heart’s rhythm and cause unconsciousness, so a precise account of what someone experiences would be speculative.

A malfunction might involve a loose electrode, improperly prepared contact material, faulty wiring, or an interrupted power supply. Instead of delivering the intended current reliably, the equipment could produce uneven heating or fail to induce unconsciousness as intended. Depending on the fault, witnesses might hear electrical arcing, notice smoke near a contact point, or see operators stop the procedure to inspect the equipment. Visible movement alone would not establish whether the person was conscious; electrical stimulation can cause involuntary movement.

The first vibration reached her through her teeth.

She had pressed her cheek to the floor beneath the bed, and the scrape traveled along the boards—a coarse, shuddering drag that made her jaw ache. Dust trembled beside her lips. Somewhere beyond the hanging quilt, the axe caught in a seam.

Silence.

She waited for the next sound until her lungs began to burn.

Then the handle creaked in his grip, and the blade lurched free.

She clamped both hands over her mouth.

Crying was supposed to be quiet if you wanted it badly enough. She had believed that until now. But her body kept trying to betray her: a hitch beneath her ribs, a tightening in her throat, breath gathering behind her palms. Tears slipped across the bridge of her nose and pooled beneath her cheek. One nostril closed. She opened her mouth against her fingers, trying to draw air through without a sound.

The footsteps moved closer.

Each one pressed a dull knock into her breastbone. Between them came the long scrape of the axe. The bed frame gave a tiny metallic tick.

She bit the inside of her cheek and held the next sob there.

A shoe appeared beneath the quilt.

The axe stopped moving.

Without the scraping, she could hear the wetness in her own breathing. She eased one finger away from her lips, slowly, hoping that would quiet it.

Above her, the mattress dipped.

The chanting began beneath the floor.

Low voices rose through the temple’s stone grates, gathering strength until the pillars seemed to hum. Above them, a second choir answered from the darkness of the gallery. Neither group sang quite in time with the other. Their overlapping syllables filled the chamber with a slow, uneasy pulse.

The prisoner lay beneath a canopy of faded blue linen. Incense drifted across his face. He watched it move, his lips forming words the chanting swallowed.

At the altar’s head, the priest unwrapped the knife.

Its obsidian blade caught no warm reflection from the braziers. Only its chipped edges shone: thin silver curves along a surface black as still water. The priest examined the point, then rested two fingers against the prisoner’s chest.

The choir fell silent.

For a moment, the ordinary sounds of the temple returned—the hiss of burning resin, a sandal scraping stone, someone coughing behind a pillar.

The priest spoke a name.

The knife descended.

Acolytes raised a length of white linen around the altar, screening the rite from the congregation. Behind it, the priest’s shadow bent to its work. The fabric trembled in the acolytes’ hands, though there was no wind.

When they lowered the screen, the prisoner’s face had been covered. The removal was complete; his heart lay beneath a folded cloth in the shallow ceremonial bowl.

The youngest acolyte stepped forward to receive it. He had rehearsed this movement for weeks, but now he nearly missed the bowl’s handles. The priest steadied it without looking at him.

Then the chanting resumed.

The acolyte carried the offering toward the open mouth of the stone god. He kept his eyes on the carved teeth, counting them, trying not to feel the weight in his hands.

He nudged the knife across the table.

“No,” she said, answering the movement rather than her own question. It came out softly, almost politely. She put both hands in her lap.

From behind the curtain came a quick, uneven breath. Mara knew that sound. Her daughter was trying not to cry. She would be waiting for her mother to say there had been a mistake, that they could get their coats now.

Mara lifted her right hand.

Her arm felt strangely heavy. She had to watch it move, had to give it instructions: across the table, fingers open. The wood caught against a rough patch of skin at her wrist. She noticed a dark ring left by someone’s cup and found herself keeping her sleeve clear of it.

Then her fingertips touched the handle.

Cold metal at the bolster. Worn wood beyond it. Her stomach tightened so abruptly that she swallowed against nausea. She tried to close her hand, but her fingers only trembled on either side of the knife.

“I need you to promise,” she said.

“Mum?”

“I’m here.”

She could say that much truthfully. She held on to the knife and looked at the blue shoe.

“You ever notice,” Eddie said, working the brush across the floor, “rich people always buy white tile?”

“They don’t expect to do their own cleaning.”

“Nobody expects to do their own cleaning. That’s how we got a pension.”

“We don’t have a pension.”

“Then what am I paying Sal for?”

“Sal’s pension.”

Eddie stopped scrubbing.

Across the kitchen, Rosa wrung out a rag. The refrigerator hummed with the confidence of an appliance that had never witnessed anything.

“This isn’t even top ten,” she said.

“I didn’t say it was.”

“You made the noise.”

“What noise?”

“That little marriage proposal you make to God.”

Eddie leaned back on his heels. “There was blood under the fruit bowl, Rosa. Under it. Fruit bowl hadn’t moved.”

“Don’t investigate. It makes the night longer.”

For a while, their brushes rasped against the tile.

“Fish market,” Eddie said.

“No.”

“You asked about disgusting.”

“I didn’t ask anything.”

“August. Power out since Friday. We get there Monday.”

Rosa shut her eyes. “I remember.”

“Guy in the office was the freshest thing in the building.”

“I remember, Eddie.”

“I threw those shoes away.”

“I threw your shoes away. You were going to put them in my car.”

“They were orthopedic.”

“They were moving.”

Eddie conceded the point with a tilt of his brush.

“What’s yours, then?”

“The wedding.”

“The wedding wasn’t bad.”

“The wedding cake.”

“Oh.”

“Five tiers. Little sugar roses. Somebody had put it back in the walk-in like the reception might resume.”

“The groom’s mother insisted.”

“She asked me to save the top tier.”

“Tradition.”

“She handed me a cake box while I was wearing those gloves.”

Eddie looked down at his hands. “Yeah. All right.”

“And then she asked whether I was with the caterer.”

“You do have a hospitality face.”

“I have a face that says pay me before I start.”

“That’s hospitality in this town.”

Rosa shifted to another patch of floor. Her knee clicked.

“I’ll tell you what was worse,” she said. “The apartment with the cats.”

Eddie’s brush stopped again.

“No.”

“You brought up the fish.”

“We agreed not to talk about the cats.”

“There were seventeen.”

“There were eighteen. One was inside the sofa.”

“Don’t.”

“You started.”

The refrigerator motor cut off. Somewhere upstairs, a phone vibrated against a hard surface, stopped, then started again.

Rosa looked toward the ceiling.

“Family?” Eddie asked.

“Probably.”

Neither moved until it stopped.

Then Eddie bent over the floor again.

“My daughter thinks I clean hotels.”

“Mine thinks I do offices.”

“Does she ask questions?”

“She asked why I work nights.”

“What’d you say?”

“Less foot traffic.”

Eddie nodded.

After a minute, he said, “Mine wants to come with me. Career day.”

“Tell her you clean fish markets.”

“She’d still come.”

Rosa glanced at him. “Then take a day off and bring her somewhere nice.”

“Sal won’t like it.”

“Put it toward his pension.”

Eddie smiled faintly and reached for the bucket.

The crowd stopped, but the people behind it didn’t.

Mara’s feet slid forward without her permission. A shoulder drove into her chest; someone’s elbow caught beneath her chin. She tried to turn sideways, to make room for one good breath, but there was nowhere to turn. Bodies pressed against her from every direction, warm and solid and impossibly heavy.

She breathed out.

She couldn’t breathe in again.

For several seconds she stayed upright only because the crowd held her there. Her shoes barely touched the pavement. Somewhere close, a man kept saying, “Please,” in a calm, bewildered voice.

Then the person beside her fell.

Mara dropped into the space they left. Her knee struck the ground, followed by her cheek. She planted a palm and tried to push herself up, but another body landed across her hips. A shoe came down between her shoulder blades.

She opened her mouth to shout. Nothing came out.

The pressure shifted. For an instant she thought she would be able to pull her knee beneath her. Then a foot landed on her side, and she felt a small, distinct crack inside her chest. Pain caught sharply when she tried to inhale. She stopped trying for half a second, frightened of it, then tried again because she had to.

Around her, shoes scraped and stumbled. She could see an untied lace dragging over the pavement. She reached for a trouser leg, caught the fabric, lost it.

Her whole attention narrowed to the shallow movement of her chest. She needed the weight off her. She needed someone to notice that she was still down there.

A hand closed around her wrist.

“Hold on.”

She gripped it with everything she had left.

The lock gave once, a small metallic complaint.

Mara watched the door from the chair beneath the window. Six floors below, a tram rounded the corner, its windows bright with people going home. One passenger had fallen asleep against the glass. Another was peeling an orange.

The lock gave again.

She had imagined there would be time to decide. Training had made the moment seem spacious: assess, choose, act. But the radio was dead, the stairwell occupied, and someone on the other side of the door had begun speaking her real name.

The cyanide pill was in her palm.

“Mara,” the voice said. “Put your hands where we can see them.”

She swallowed before the sentence ended.

For a moment nothing changed.

The tram continued along its tracks. The radiator clicked. She became aware of a loose thread at her cuff and reached to pull it free.

Then her stomach tightened. Heat rose abruptly through her chest, followed by a dizziness that made the window seem to slide sideways. She gripped the arms of the chair. Her breathing grew quick and unsatisfying; each breath felt unfinished.

She tried to sit straighter.

Her body would not quite obey.

This was what the instructors had left out: after the decision, there would still be a person here. Someone frightened by the hammering in her chest. Someone watching her own fingers tremble and wanting them to stop.

The door shook in its frame.

She wanted to say something. Not a password or a warning. Perhaps only wait.

But waiting was no longer something anyone could give her.

The realization came cold and plain. She would not reach the safe house. She would not retrieve the coat she had left at the station. Her sister would keep wondering whether the last unanswered letter had offended her.

There would be no opportunity to explain that it hadn’t.

The door burst inward. A man shouted. Another knelt beside her, pulling off his gloves, and she looked at him with sudden, helpless attention.

He was trying to help.

She had not imagined that part either.

Beyond his shoulder, through the open doorway, she could see an ordinary hallway: scuffed paint, a crooked light fixture, muddy footprints on the carpet. She fixed her eyes on it as the room dimmed, wanting, with all the strength she had left, to stand up and walk out.

The footsteps stopped when I stopped.

I stood beneath the last working streetlamp on Bellweather Road, pretending to search my bag for my keys. Behind me, beyond the yellow circle of light, something shifted its weight on the pavement.

“Go on, then,” I said, without turning. “I know you’re there.”

A man stepped out from between two parked cars.

He wore a gray coat, buttoned wrong. One lapel stood up against his cheek. I’d noticed him outside the pharmacy, then again reflected in the dark window of the laundromat.

Now he was close enough that I could see his feet were bare.

“You should get inside,” he said.

My keys slipped through my fingers and struck the pavement.

He flinched at the sound. His whole body tightened, and for a moment he looked less like someone threatening me than someone trying desperately not to be sick.

Then his jaw cracked.

I heard it distinctly: a hard, dry snap. His mouth fell open too far, and he caught his chin in both hands.

I backed into the streetlamp.

“No,” he said into his palms.

The next crack came from his shoulder.

It rose beneath his coat, pushing the fabric into a sharp peak. He staggered against a car, denting the door with his hip. The alarm chirped once and began to shriek.

He dropped to his knees.

I should have run then. Instead I watched his fingers spread against the road. They kept spreading. The joints lifted one after another, knuckles swelling as the bones lengthened beneath the skin. His nails scraped the asphalt, thickening into dark hooks.

He looked up at me.

His eyes were still human. That was what held me there.

They were wet and terrified, fixed on mine as his face began to change around them.

His nose flattened, then pushed forward. The skin beside his mouth stretched tight enough to shine beneath the streetlight. His lips drew back from teeth that no longer fit behind them. I heard a series of small clicks as his jaw shifted, followed by a grinding sound I felt in my own molars.

He tried to speak.

Only the first syllable came out clearly.

“R—”

His spine arched.

The coat strained across his back. A seam split under one arm, exposing pale skin covered in gooseflesh. Dark hair pressed through it, sparse at first, then so thick I could no longer see the skin beneath. His shoulders widened inside the ruined coat.

I bent for my keys without taking my eyes off him. My fingertips brushed cold metal, pushed it away, found it again.

His legs folded wrong.

There was no other way my mind could make sense of it. He braced on his hands while his heels lifted and his calves tightened. Something broke with a muffled crunch. He shuddered, dragging deep breaths through his lengthening muzzle.

I ran.

The entrance to my building was six houses away. I counted them because I couldn’t bear to listen behind me.

Five.

A car alarm. My shoes. My breath.

Four.

Claws struck pavement.

Three.

I reached my door, missed the lock, and drove the key into the painted wood beside it.

Behind me, the running stopped.

I found the lock.

As I turned the key, a warm breath moved through my hair.

Then, very gently, something caught the back of my coat.

The footsteps stopped when I stopped.

I stood beneath the last working streetlamp on Bellweather Road, pretending to search my bag for my keys. Behind me, beyond the yellow circle of light, something shifted its weight on the pavement.

“Go on, then,” I said, without turning. “I know you’re there.”

A man stepped out from between two parked cars.

He wore a gray coat, buttoned wrong. One lapel stood up against his cheek. I’d noticed him outside the pharmacy, then again reflected in the dark window of the laundromat.

Now he was close enough that I could see his feet were bare.

“You should get inside,” he said.

My keys slipped through my fingers and struck the pavement.

He flinched at the sound. His whole body tightened, and for a moment he looked less like someone threatening me than someone trying desperately not to be sick.

Then his jaw cracked.

I heard it distinctly: a hard, dry snap. His mouth fell open too far, and he caught his chin in both hands.

I backed into the streetlamp.

“No,” he said into his palms.

The next crack came from his shoulder.

It rose beneath his coat, pushing the fabric into a sharp peak. He staggered against a car, denting the door with his hip. The alarm chirped once and began to shriek.

He dropped to his knees.

I should have run then. Instead I watched his fingers spread against the road. They kept spreading. The joints lifted one after another, knuckles swelling as the bones lengthened beneath the skin. His nails scraped the asphalt, thickening into dark hooks.

He looked up at me.

His eyes were still human. That was what held me there.

They were wet and terrified, fixed on mine as his face began to change around them.

His nose flattened, then pushed forward. The skin beside his mouth stretched tight enough to shine beneath the streetlight. His lips drew back from teeth that no longer fit behind them. I heard a series of small clicks as his jaw shifted, followed by a grinding sound I felt in my own molars.

He tried to speak.

Only the first syllable came out clearly.

“R—”

His spine arched.

The coat strained across his back. A seam split under one arm, exposing pale skin covered in gooseflesh. Dark hair pressed through it, sparse at first, then so thick I could no longer see the skin beneath. His shoulders widened inside the ruined coat.

I bent for my keys without taking my eyes off him. My fingertips brushed cold metal, pushed it away, found it again.

His legs folded wrong.

There was no other way my mind could make sense of it. He braced on his hands while his heels lifted and his calves tightened. Something broke with a muffled crunch. He shuddered, dragging deep breaths through his lengthening muzzle.

I ran.

The entrance to my building was six houses away. I counted them because I couldn’t bear to listen behind me.

Five.

A car alarm. My shoes. My breath.

Four.

Claws struck pavement.

Three.

I reached my door, missed the lock, and drove the key into the painted wood beside it.

Behind me, the running stopped.

I found the lock.

As I turned the key, a warm breath moved through my hair.

Then, very gently, something caught the back of my coat.

I can convey the speed and terror of an early Victorian operation, but not graphic surgical gore.

The surgeon looked once at the clock.

“Hold him steady.”

Two assistants braced the patient against the narrow table. He had begged while they arranged the instruments; now, seeing the surgeon take his place, he fell abruptly silent.

What followed was swift, practiced work. The surgeon’s shoulders scarcely moved. He issued instructions in clipped syllables, never looking up, and each instrument was waiting when he reached for it.

The patient cried out. A student near the doorway went pale but remained where he stood.

“Nearly finished,” an assistant said, close to the patient’s ear.

The surgeon did not repeat the reassurance. He concentrated on finishing, then called for dressings.

Only when the immediate work was done did anyone glance at the clock again. Less than two minutes had passed. The patient lay trembling as the assistants loosened their hold.

results.model_response:
By sunset, Mara could no longer remember her daughter’s name.

She remembered other things. The blue house beside the overpass. The dent in its mailbox. How her daughter used to leave a spoon in the sugar bowl, though Mara had asked her a thousand times not to.

“Starts with an E,” she said.

“June,” Tomas told her.

Mara looked down at the bite on her wrist. They had wrapped it in a dish towel printed with lemons. Blood had darkened the yellow fruit.

“That’s right.”

Across the room, Eli pressed his palms against his eyes.

The four of them had dragged a wardrobe in front of the schoolroom door. Outside, somewhere in the corridor, a loose window knocked in its frame. For two hours they had listened to it, grateful for any sound they didn’t have to make themselves.

“We could wait,” Eli said.

No one answered.

“She’s still here.”

“I know,” Tomas said.

“You don’t know. You’ve been checking that gun since we got inside.”

Tomas put the pistol on a desk.

There was a child’s name carved into the wood beneath it: BEN. Someone had spent a long time digging the letters deep.

Ruth sat beside Mara on the floor. She had not let go of Mara’s uninjured hand.

“We saw what happened to Ansel,” Ruth said.

“Ansel was sick before—”

“We saw.”

Eli turned toward the boarded windows. He was seventeen. Three months ago, Mara had found him hiding in a delivery van and persuaded the others to spend half a tank of fuel taking him along.

Now he said, “We could tie her up.”

Mara lifted her head.

“Please don’t.”

“We wouldn’t leave you.”

“I know you wouldn’t.”

“We could stay right here.”

“Eli.”

He stopped.

She waited until he looked at her. Her eyes were still her eyes, which was the unbearable thing.

“Come sit down.”

He crossed the room reluctantly and lowered himself beside her, careful not to touch the towel.

For a while, nobody spoke.

Mara began to shiver. Ruth pulled a coat around her shoulders, then tucked the loose cuff under her chin with an unnecessary tenderness. There was no way to make her comfortable now, but Ruth kept trying.

“Tell me again,” Mara said.

“June.”

“June.” She tested the name. “She hated when I brushed her hair.”

“You told us.”

“I wasn’t gentle enough.”

Ruth shook her head.

“I was always in a hurry.”

Tomas looked at the ceiling. A paper solar system hung there, its planets bleached pale by years of sunlight. Earth had fallen from its string and lay beneath a chair.

“We should decide,” he said.

Eli stared at him. “You mean we should say yes so you don’t have to decide.”

Tomas opened his mouth, then closed it.

“Yes,” he said at last. “I suppose I do.”

The loose window knocked twice.

Mara watched them. “I want you to do it while I can still ask.”

Ruth bent over their joined hands.

“I can’t say it,” she whispered.

“You don’t have to.”

“But you’ll think I didn’t—”

“I won’t.”

Eli was crying without trying to hide it now. He wiped his nose on his sleeve and took Mara’s other hand, just above the wrist.

Tomas picked up the pistol.

Then he stood holding it at his side, unable to move.

Mara saw.

“All right,” she said, though nothing was.

He knelt in front of her. Up close, he could smell the orange peel she kept in her pocket because she liked the smell and because, she said, liking something was reason enough to carry it.

“Do you want us to go?” Ruth asked.

“No.”

So they stayed.

Mara asked them to tell June that she had tried to get home. Nobody reminded her that June was dead. Ruth promised. Eli promised twice.

Tomas leaned forward and kissed Mara’s forehead.

She shut her eyes.

He waited for her to open them again. He wanted another instruction, or a refusal. Anything that would give him something else to do.

“Tomas,” she said.

He did not make her ask again.

The shot filled the little room.

Afterward, Eli kept holding her hand.

Tomas set the pistol on the floor and pushed it away. He could hear Ruth breathing in short, careful breaths beside him. In the corridor, the window struck its frame again.

Nobody moved when darkness reached them.

Eventually, Ruth loosened Mara’s fingers from Eli’s. He resisted at first, then helped her lay the hand in Mara’s lap.

“June,” he said suddenly.

They looked at him.

“Her daughter’s name was June.”

“We know,” Ruth said.

He nodded, but a moment later he said it again.

results.model_response:
For the first week, the dead man was only a mistake in the light.

A coat hanging beside a doorway. Someone waiting across the street, gone when the bus passed. The narrow darkness between the refrigerator and the wall.

Daniel never saw him directly. That was the rule, although he did not yet think of it as a rule. He would catch the suggestion of a shoulder, the pale oval of a face, and turn to find something ordinary.

Lack of sleep, he decided.

He bought new bulbs for the hallway. He stopped hanging clothes over chairs.

For a while, this helped.

The murder itself remained strangely manageable. He remembered it as a sequence of practical problems: the sound, the weight, the time. There were details he could examine without feeling anything at all. He could recall which hand he had used to close the door. He could remember being annoyed that his sleeve had caught on the latch.

What troubled him was an earlier moment.

The man had bent to retrieve a glove he’d dropped.

Daniel could not understand why this memory kept returning. Nothing important had happened then. There had still been time.

By the second month, he had begun arranging rooms around what he could not bear to see.

He moved his desk so that his back faced the wall. He took down the mirror opposite his bed. At restaurants he asked for corner tables, then stopped going to restaurants because the windows reflected people who weren’t behind him.

His friends noticed his exhaustion.

“Work,” he said.

It was such a useful answer that he began resenting them for accepting it.

The figure grew more definite as everything else became uncertain. Daniel forgot appointments, misplaced money, read the same paragraph until the words lost their meaning. But he knew the precise angle at which the dead man held his head. He knew that the left shoulder sat slightly lower than the right.

Once, brushing his teeth, he saw him in the doorway through the edge of the mirror.

Daniel kept brushing.

His eyes watered. Foam slipped onto his wrist. He stared at his own mouth and continued the small, obedient movement of his hand.

Only when his arm began to ache did he turn.

The doorway was empty.

After that, he found reasons not to brush his teeth.

The deterioration was mostly undramatic. Unopened envelopes accumulated beneath the letterbox. Milk spoiled in the refrigerator. He wore the same shirt for four days because choosing another required him to open the wardrobe, and the wardrobe was one of the places.

He began saying things aloud to establish that they were true.

“I’m making coffee.”

“It’s Tuesday.”

“There’s nobody in the kitchen.”

The last sentence became difficult. Sometimes he had to say it from the hallway.

He tried, once, to apologize.

He had been sitting on the bed when he noticed the familiar shape beside the window. He kept his gaze fixed on his knees.

“I’m sorry.”

Nothing happened.

He waited, humiliated by the silence. Then anger came so suddenly that he stood up.

“What do you want me to do?”

The window held only his reflection.

He closed the curtains and spent the rest of the night explaining himself to the room. At first he spoke carefully, presenting the circumstances in order. By dawn he was repeating a single sentence whose meaning had worn away.

It hadn’t been like that.

Eventually he stopped turning to look.

The effort was too great, and the brief relief of finding an empty corner had become unbearable. Better to let the figure remain where it was. Better to eat with someone standing beside the cupboard than spend another evening proving, every few seconds, that he was alone.

One morning he made two cups of coffee.

He noticed only after setting them on the table.

For a long time he stood looking at the second cup. Then he sat down opposite it, keeping his eyes lowered, and waited for it to cool.

The room was dry. That was the fact Daniel kept trying to hold.

Dry walls. Dry concrete. A pale crescent of dust beneath the door.

Then the water came, and facts stopped helping.

He knew he wasn’t in the river. Somewhere beyond the cloth covering his face, a chair scraped against the floor. A man coughed. Ordinary sounds, belonging to a room with air in it.

But he could not find that air.

His body fought before he could think. The restraints caught him; the table creaked. He had been frightened before—under artillery, in the wreck of the truck—but those fears had left room for decisions. Take cover. Stay still. Run.

This left room for nothing.

When they paused, he heard himself making a sound he didn’t recognize. He wanted to stop it. He had imagined, before capture, that dignity was something a person could choose.

“Where is the communications post?”

He knew the answer. For a moment he could see it clearly: the narrow cellar, the signal lamp, Petrov eating an apple with his headset crooked over one ear.

Then someone moved near his head.

“No,” Daniel said.

He hadn’t meant to say anything. The word escaped on its own.

“Where?”

His eyes searched what little he could see. A sleeve. The edge of a light fixture. Water running toward a crack in the floor. He fixed on the crack, trying to remember that water ran downward, that the floor was beneath him, that he was not sinking.

He tried to count. He reached three and forgot what came next.

They hadn’t started again. That was worse in a way he could never have explained: the waiting had already taken possession of his body. Each small movement in the room made him flinch. He listened for the vessel being lifted. He listened so hard he almost missed the question.

“Tell us.”

Daniel opened his mouth. He wanted to ask them to remove the cloth. He wanted to say he needed a minute, just one uninterrupted minute.

What came out was “Please.”

Beneath the door, the crescent of dust was still dry.

The bounty on Elias Venn was worth enough to buy Mara a new spine.

Not a better ship. Not a month somewhere with real sunlight. Just a spine that didn’t click whenever the weather systems over Europa changed pressure.

She found him beneath the midnight market, waiting beside a freight capsule with a stolen face flickering across his features.

“Elias,” she said.

The face settled on that of an elderly woman.

“Wrong person.”

“You’ve still got your own shoes.”

He looked down.

Mara drew her stun pistol. “Hands where I can see them.”

For a moment, all she heard was the market overhead: footsteps, vendors, rain drumming against the dome. Then Venn kicked a stack of empty coolant cans between them and ran.

Mara followed him into the freight passage. Her spine clicked.

“That,” she muttered, “is coming out of your deposit.”

Venn reached the capsule first. He slapped its controls, but Mara’s warrant had already frozen every public transit lock in the district.

He turned with a utility knife in his hand.

“Don’t,” Mara said.

“You don’t know who’s paying you.”

“I know who wants you alive.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

He lunged.

Mara stepped back and fired.

Two tethered contacts caught his jacket, their barbs punching through to the skin. The pistol delivered a brief train of high-voltage pulses.

Venn’s body stiffened mid-stride. The current disrupted the signals controlling his muscles, forcing them into rapid, involuntary contractions. His arm jerked inward; the knife struck the floor. His knees stopped carrying him, and he fell hard against the capsule door before sliding down.

He tried to shout. Only a strained sound escaped as his chest and abdominal muscles tightened. Pain crowded out everything else—not heat, not quite, but a violent cramping that seized several parts of his body at once. He remained conscious. That was apparent in his eyes, tracking Mara even while he could not make his limbs obey.

She released the trigger.

The rigid tension broke. Venn dragged in a breath, then another, uneven and fast. His hands trembled against the floor. Where the contacts had struck, tiny burns marked the skin beneath his torn jacket.

Mara kicked the knife away and crouched beside him.

“Can you breathe?”

He nodded, coughing.

The pistol’s display flashed an elevated pulse warning. These weapons were sold as less-lethal, which Mara knew was a promise with a footnote: abnormal heart rhythms, breathing problems, injuries from the fall. She summoned a medical drone before fastening the restraints.

Venn watched her through wet eyes.

“There’s a recorder,” he whispered. “Inside my left heel.”

Mara paused with one hand on his shoe.

“Evidence?”

“Why they want me.”

Above them, someone in the market began playing a battered saxophone. The tune drifted through the ventilation grilles.

Mara removed the heel and slipped the little data wafer into her pocket.

“You’re still coming with me,” she said.

Venn closed his eyes.

“But first,” she added, as the medical drone rounded the corner, “we’re taking a different route.”

results.model_response:
When Mara woke, the room was already counting down.

Red numbers burned above a steel door: **04:59**.

She tried to stand. The cuff around her wrist snapped her back into the chair.

For a few seconds, she refused to understand the arrangement. A lever beneath her free hand. A slot enclosing her other arm. The green word **RELEASE** printed beside a diagram she looked at once and then could not look at again.

A speaker clicked.

“The door opens when you finish.”

Mara waited for more. Instructions. An accusation. Some explanation she could argue with.

The speaker went quiet.

**04:31**.

“No,” she said.

She searched the chair with her free hand, feeling beneath the seat, along the welded joints, around the bolts securing it to the floor. She pulled at the cuff until the whole assembly rattled. There had to be something overlooked. A loose screw. A cable she could reach. Something made by a person who had been tired or careless.

There was nothing she could move except the lever.

**03:48**.

She shouted for help. Then she shouted threats. Each time she stopped, she listened so hard that the hum of the lights seemed to swell.

At last she looked at the diagram again.

Her stomach clenched. She turned her face away and swallowed repeatedly, concentrating on not being sick. Sweat cooled beneath her shirt. Her trapped hand had begun to tremble, and seeing it tremble frightened her more than the machine. Until then, some part of her had believed she might become a different person when the time came—calm, decisive, capable of doing what was necessary.

She was still herself.

She wanted someone to arrive and tell her she didn’t have to.

**02:56**.

Mara put her free hand on the lever. Its grip was warm from the room.

She took it off.

“Not yet.”

The words brought a moment’s relief. Then she saw the timer and understood what that relief was costing her.

She moved her feet beneath the chair, then moved them back. Tried sitting upright. Tried closing her eyes. Nothing made the next few seconds imaginable. She kept anticipating a courage that did not come.

In her kitchen, miles away, there was a mug beside the sink. She had left a little coffee in it. By now there would be a brown line around the inside.

The thought was so ordinary that she began to cry.

**01:39**.

She wiped her face against her shoulder. She needed to see the door.

Her hand returned to the lever, awkward and damp. She could feel herself preparing to snatch it away again.

“I don’t want to,” she whispered.

No answer came. She hadn’t expected one, but she listened anyway.

Then she looked past the diagram, past the steel surrounding her wrist, and fixed her eyes on the narrow gap beneath the door.

There was light on the other side.

Mara began to move the lever.

results.model_response:
The plank complained beneath Tomas’s bare feet.

Behind him, the ship creaked at anchor. No one spoke. Even the men who had whispered mutiny with him now watched from behind the captain, their faces carefully empty.

Captain Vale rested one hand on the rail.

“You wanted command,” she said. “There’s your quarterdeck.”

Tomas looked down.

The water was so clear he could see the pale sand far beneath the keel. A dark shape passed over it, long and slow. Then another crossed beneath the first.

A fin broke the surface beside the plank.

Tomas stepped backward before he could stop himself. The point of a cutlass touched his shirt.

“Forward,” said the boatswain.

“Captain.” His voice came out thin. He swallowed and tried again. “Captain, I’ll take the lash.”

Vale said nothing.

“Put me ashore. No water, no knife. Give me that much.”

One of the sharks turned beneath him. He watched its tail move from side to side, the effortless correction of its body. It disappeared under the ship, and Tomas found that worse than seeing it.

He searched the faces along the rail.

Hobb had shared his tobacco that morning. Mercer owed him six silver pieces. Young Bell had followed him through the powder smoke at Saint Kitts, clutching Tomas’s coat like a frightened child.

Bell looked away.

The boatswain pressed the cutlass forward.

Tomas took another step. The board dipped, and he flung out his arms. A small sound escaped him—a gasp almost like a laugh. He had stood steady on yardarms in a gale. Now, with land in sight and hardly a ripple on the sea, his knees would not obey him.

“There’s still time,” he said.

For a moment he thought Vale might answer.

She glanced instead toward the men at the rail.

Tomas understood then that she needed them watching.

At the end of the plank, there was barely room for both his feet. Sunlight struck the water hard enough to hurt his eyes. He tried to watch the horizon, but his gaze kept falling to the circling shapes below.

“Please,” he said, no longer certain whom he meant.

The board shifted behind him.

He caught one last glimpse of the ship: tarred ropes, a patched sail, Bell with both hands over his mouth.

Then Tomas reached for the plank, missed it, and fell.

The splash sounded small beside the hull. Every man at the rail leaned forward.

Captain Vale alone remained where she was.

At first, Mara thought the pressure around her ribs was someone’s arm.

Then she looked down.

The device sat against her sternum, squat and heavy, held in place by straps that pulled her shirt into tight wrinkles. Wires disappeared beneath its casing. One brushed the hollow of her throat whenever she breathed.

Tick.

She stopped breathing.

Tick.

The sound was small and dry. That was the worst of it. Not an alarm, not anything that belonged to an emergency. Just a patient little click, loud enough to hear in the empty room.

“No,” she said.

She touched a wire with the tip of one finger. Its plastic coating was smooth and cold, except for a rough seam that caught against her skin. She snatched her hand away. Now she could still feel it on her fingertip.

Tick.

“Okay. Okay.”

She tried to stand, but the weight shifted against her chest and she sat down hard. A buckle pressed into her side. Beneath the straps, sweat gathered and made her shirt cling. Every shallow breath dragged fabric across skin; every deeper breath met resistance.

She spread her hands on her knees to keep them still. They wouldn’t stay there.

“Somebody?”

Her voice barely reached the door.

Tick.

She stared at the wires, trying to remember whether that loose curve had been there a moment ago. Had she moved it? Had she pulled something when she stood?

“Somebody help me.”

Her fingers crept toward the straps. She caught her own wrist and squeezed until it hurt.

The next tick seemed late.

She waited, mouth open, unable to draw air.

Tick.

A sob burst out of her. Then she was shouting, pitching forward despite herself, shouting at the door while the casing knocked against her breastbone.

“Please. Please, come in. Don’t leave me here.”

The hall light didn’t come on.

Mara flicked the switch twice more, listening to the small plastic click. The refrigerator was still humming in the kitchen. Through the front window, the porch light shone on the wet steps.

“Great,” she whispered.

She left her shoes by the door and went down the hall in damp socks, one hand against the wall. Her phone was in her bag, under the umbrella and the groceries she’d bought on the way home. It wasn’t worth digging out just to get upstairs.

Behind the half-open dining room door, a man stood with his back against the wall.

He had heard her key before he could find a way out. Now he held a kitchen knife close to his thigh, the blade pointed down. He watched her pass through the narrow gap between the door and its frame.

Mara caught her foot on something.

She lurched forward, struck the wall with her palm, and felt a sharp pain in her smallest toe.

“Shit.”

A shoe. One of her running shoes, lying in the middle of the hall.

She nudged it toward the skirting board. She must have kicked it there that morning. She remembered being late, looking for her headphones, carrying a piece of toast from room to room.

Still, she paused.

The house smelled faintly of rain.

Not the familiar wet-wool smell rising from her own coat. Something colder: soaked concrete, damp leaves.

She looked toward the kitchen.

The back door was open an inch.

For several seconds she didn’t move. She could see the pale vertical line between the door and the frame. At its base, rain had darkened the mat.

Had she taken the recycling out before work?

She tried to remember doing it. The bin lid. The stiff latch. Pulling the door hard because it swelled in wet weather.

She could remember all those things, but not whether they had happened today.

Behind her, the man shifted his grip. His palm was sweating. The knife handle made a faint tacky sound against his skin.

Mara turned.

Nothing moved in the hall.

“Hello?”

Her voice was too quiet. She cleared her throat.

“Is someone here?”

The refrigerator stopped humming.

In the sudden quiet, she heard water ticking from the kitchen tap.

She stood with her arms close to her sides, looking back toward the front door. Her bag sat beneath the coat hooks, perhaps six steps away.

The dining room door was between her and it.

She couldn’t remember leaving that open, either.

For a moment she considered running upstairs and locking herself in the bathroom. Then she pictured the bathroom lock, the little brass bolt that never quite lined up, and stayed where she was.

Her keys were still in her coat pocket.

She slipped her hand inside slowly. Metal touched her fingertips. She closed her fist around the keys to keep them from jingling.

“I’m going back out,” she said.

She had meant to sound as though she were speaking to someone on the phone. Instead, it sounded like a request.

The man watched the shape of her hand inside her pocket.

Mara took one step toward the front door.

The floorboard creaked beneath her heel. She stopped, angry with herself for stopping. It was her floor. She knew that board creaked.

Another step.

As she came level with the dining room, she kept her eyes on her bag. If she looked into the room, she thought, she would have to see whatever was there.

Her coat sleeve brushed the edge of the door.

It moved inward.

Someone caught it before it could touch the wall.

Mara saw the fingers first.

Then she ran.
