The hotel charged extra for a sea view, which seemed dishonest to Mara. Between the window and the sea stood a parking garage, a billboard for dental implants, and another hotel.

“You can see it if you stand on the bed,” Ellis said.

“I’m not standing on the bed.”

“Then you’re choosing not to see it.”

Mara sat at the little writing desk, wiping fingerprints from the blade of a knife. Ellis had spread a towel over the coffee table and was cleaning his pistol beneath a lamp shaped like a pineapple.

For a while, there was only the whisper of cloth on metal and the television next door, where someone was apparently winning an argument with a studio audience.

“What’s your favorite?” Ellis asked.

“Hotel?”

“No. Way.”

Mara looked at the pistol on his towel.

“Bit personal.”

“We’ve worked together six years.”

“And maintained a healthy professional distance.”

“You ate half my omelet this morning.”

“You said you were finished.”

“I said I was devastated.”

“You should speak more precisely.”

Ellis smiled and went back to work.

Mara held the knife toward the lamp, inspected it, then lowered it again.

“Quiet,” she said.

“Quiet isn’t a way.”

“It’s a criterion.”

“Knife, then.”

“Sometimes.”

“Too intimate for me.”

“You’re a surprisingly squeamish man.”

“I don’t like people breathing on me. That was true before I got into this.”

Mara folded her cloth into a smaller square. “Yours?”

“Rifle.”

“Predictable.”

“Comfortable shoes are predictable. I like those too.”

“You complained about the last one.”

“I complained about the rain.”

“And the walk.”

“It was a long walk.”

“And a bird.”

Ellis stopped polishing. “That bird had a problem with me.”

“It was nesting.”

“It made its position very clear.”

Mara’s mouth twitched.

He pointed at her with the cloth. “There. That’s why I ask these questions. Otherwise we sit here like a miserable married couple.”

“A miserable married couple would have booked the sea view on points.”

From next door came a burst of applause.

Ellis glanced toward the wall. “Ever tried poison?”

“No.”

“Really?”

“I like cooking. I want one thing in my life to stay pleasant.”

“That’s almost wholesome.”

“Don’t spread it around.”

He set his pistol down on the towel and leaned back. The pineapple lamp threw a patchwork of yellow light over his shirt.

“I used to have an answer,” he said.

“You just said rifle.”

“No, I mean a proper favorite. Something I looked forward to.”

Mara stopped wiping the blade.

“The work?”

“The bit after. Breakfast, usually. Finding somewhere that did breakfast all day.”

“You still do that.”

“Now I get indigestion.”

She considered him for a moment, then put the knife away.

“That’ll be the onions.”

“Probably.”

A trolley rattled past in the corridor. Both of them listened until it had gone.

Ellis picked up the room-service menu.

“They do pancakes.”

“At eleven at night?”

“All day.”

“Optimistic.”

He reached for the telephone, then hesitated.

“Are you finished?”

Mara looked at the bare desk, the folded cloth in her hand.

“Yes.”

“Good. Because I’m ordering you your own this time.”

She rose and crossed to the window. After a moment, she took off her shoes and stepped onto the bed.

“Well?” Ellis asked.

Beyond the parking garage, a narrow black strip caught the lights of a passing ship.

“Sea,” she said.

“Told you.”

“Still not worth thirty euros.”

The heat reached them before the flames, tightening the air until every breath felt drawn from an opened furnace. They pulled against the ropes by instinct, though there was nowhere on the narrow platform to go. At their feet, green wood hissed and snapped.

“I’m not a witch.”

The first time, the words were clear. The second time, coughing broke them apart. They called for someone in the crowd—a name, repeated urgently—and then their voice rose into a scream.

People who had watched without moving lowered their eyes. The prayer stopped. Their last cry was scarcely louder than the crackling wood, but in the silence around the stake, it carried.

The first soldier rose facing backward.

His knees bent as they should. His hands gripped the mud. But his head hung between his shoulder blades, and when he climbed from the trench, he stood patiently with his face turned toward the grave.

Veyr watched him for a moment.

“That will do,” she said.

She set the iron bell upon the altar. It had no clapper. She had cut that out herself, along with the tongue of the man who cast it, for this work required an instrument that could not honestly make a sound.

When she rang it, the valley answered.

Mud trembled across the burial field. Grave markers leaned toward her: wooden stakes, broken swords, stones placed by hands that had since gone cold themselves. Beneath them, something vast shifted—not a body, but the agreement by which bodies remained still.

Veyr opened her book.

The pages were blank until she looked away. Then words appeared at the edges of her sight, crowding together like insects beneath a lifted stone. She read them without turning her eyes.

The second soldier came up through the roots of an elder tree.

Rot had softened his face into a loose, gray mask. One cheek clung to the bark as he pulled free. His mail hung over a hollow belly, its rings furred with rust; through the gaps, pale threads of fungus shivered in air that had suddenly become warm.

More hands broke the earth.

Some still wore gloves. Some were little more than finger bones held together by blackened cords. They clawed upward with the mindless care of sleepers rearranging their blankets.

The smell reached Veyr a moment later: wet wool, cellar mold, the thick sweetness of flesh kept too long beneath summer soil. She pressed a scented cloth beneath her nose, then lowered it. She needed both hands for the next verse.

She spoke the names of seven forgotten gods in the order of their deaths.

The stars moved.

Only a little. Only enough that every shadow in the valley pointed toward a different sky.

A corpse near the altar began to weep. Dark water ran from its empty sockets. Beside it, a dead horse struggled upright, its rider still pinned beneath the saddle. Neither made a sound.

Veyr’s apprentice stepped back.

He had prepared himself for the bodies. He had spent three days uncovering them, loosening buckles and cutting roots away from wrists. Now he stared at his own shadow. It had remained beside the altar when he moved.

“Master.”

“Keep counting.”

“I can’t.”

She glanced up.

Across the field, the dead were standing in rows. There were more of them than they had buried. Between men he recognized, the apprentice saw tall, shrouded figures lifting themselves from patches of earth his spade had never touched.

One raised a hand to him.

He almost raised his own.

Veyr caught his wrist and pressed it back to the open ledger.

“Keep counting,” she said again.

Then she rang the silent bell, and the army turned toward the road.

The warehouse door shut behind Nico, cutting off the streetlight.

Vega stood beside a man seated on the concrete floor. His wrists were tied. One shoe was missing. He looked older than Nico’s father.

“He talked to people he shouldn’t,” Vega said.

Nico had been told this was a meeting. He looked toward the door, but the two men who had brought him were standing in front of it.

Vega held out a length of pipe.

For a moment, Nico left it hanging between them.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Then take it.”

The metal was cold enough that Nico could feel it through his sleeve. Around him, the others stopped talking. He had spent months trying to get their attention; now he wanted them to look anywhere else.

The man on the floor shook his head. “I don’t know you.”

Nico glanced at Vega.

“That’s right,” Vega said. “You don’t owe him anything.”

Someone behind Nico laughed, briefly.

He tried to hand the pipe back. Vega didn’t move.

“We fed you. Kept you safe. You said you wanted to be family.” His voice stayed level. “Was that a lie?”

“No.”

“Show me.”

Nico stepped forward. The man tried to shuffle away, dragging his bound hands across the floor.

The first blow knocked him sideways. Nico recoiled with him.

“Again,” Vega said.

“He’s down.”

“I can see that.”

Nico looked around for someone to intervene. One man watched with folded arms. Another checked his phone. At the door, neither guard moved.

The captive was crying now, struggling to draw breath quietly, as though silence might make them forget him.

“Finish proving it,” Vega said.

Nico obeyed.

When Vega finally caught his wrist, Nico nearly dropped the pipe. The man on the floor no longer tried to move away.

A hand settled on Nico’s shoulder.

“There,” Vega said. “Now we know.”

The others welcomed him with handshakes. Nico answered because they were still watching. Behind them, the injured man asked for water, and nobody turned around.

By the time he tasted the soup, I had forgotten every cruel thing he had ever done.

This struck me as unfair. For years I had kept an exact account: every humiliation, every threat delivered softly enough to pass for advice. Yet now, watching him lift the spoon, I could remember only how he used to blow across my tea when I was small.

“Too much salt,” he said.

“I’ll tell Mrs. Vale.”

“Don’t bother. She’ll take it personally.”

He dipped his spoon again.

Rain tapped the dining-room windows. Between us, the candles burned with a steadiness that seemed arranged. I had expected something in the room to object—a glass to crack, a door to bang open—but the clock continued its discreet work on the mantel.

He began discussing the orchard.

“The lower field should be sold. No sense keeping land that won’t earn.”

“Mother liked the trees.”

“Your mother liked a great many expensive things.”

There. I tried to hold on to that.

He ate another spoonful and asked whether I had spoken to the solicitor.

“Tuesday,” I said.

“You said Monday before.”

“Then Monday.”

He looked at me over the bowl. Even now, I wanted to correct myself properly, to give him an answer he would accept.

His spoon paused halfway to his mouth.

At first he appeared merely distracted. He swallowed, moved his tongue against his teeth, then reached for his water. The glass clicked against the edge of the bowl.

“Is it warm in here?”

“A little.”

“Open a window.”

I stood. At the window, my fingers slipped on the latch. Behind me he cleared his throat once, then again, harder.

Outside, the garden smelled of wet earth. I stayed there until he asked what I was doing.

“Nothing.”

“Well, sit down.”

When I returned, he had pushed the soup away.

A fine moisture shone along his upper lip. He drew his handkerchief from his pocket and pressed it to his forehead, irritated by the necessity.

“Indigestion,” he said.

“Perhaps.”

He watched me.

“What does that mean?”

“Only perhaps.”

He started to answer, but stopped. His lips tightened. One hand settled against his stomach beneath the table, and for several seconds he breathed carefully through his nose.

I could have rung the bell. The cord hung beside my chair, its tassel brushing the wallpaper.

He reached for the water again. This time his hand trembled visibly. He steadied the glass with his other hand, took a small drink, and set it down too quickly. Water spread across the cloth.

“Get someone.”

I did not move.

He stared at the spill, then at my hands folded in my lap.

“Did you hear me?”

“Yes.”

His chair scraped back. He tried to stand, caught the table edge, and sat heavily. The candle flames leaned toward him and straightened.

For the first time that evening, he said my name without annoyance.

I looked up.

His face had lost its color. He seemed to be struggling both to draw breath and to decide what to ask. His mouth opened; nothing came. Then he looked at his bowl.

I had imagined this moment so often that I recognized almost none of it. In my imagining, I had explained. He had understood. There had been room for everything I needed to say.

Instead, he reached across the table.

I took his hand before I thought about it.

His fingers closed around mine, weakly at first, then with an effort that hurt. I could not tell whether he was asking me to stay or trying to keep me from leaving.

Beside my shoulder, within easy reach, the bell cord hung still.

The plank dipped beneath Merrick’s bare feet.

Behind him, the crew had gone silent. No jeering now, no wagers passed from palm to palm. There was only the creak of timber and the small, regular slap of water against the hull.

Captain Vale stood beside the rail with Merrick’s knife in her hand.

“You asked the men to choose another captain,” she said. “They’ve chosen.”

Merrick looked back. He searched the faces nearest him—Jonah, who had shared his tobacco; Finch, whose fever he had nursed through the crossing. Finch lowered his eyes.

“Captain.” His voice broke on the word. He swallowed. “Put me ashore.”

Vale said nothing.

A gray fin surfaced beyond the plank, cut a leisurely curve through the blue, and disappeared.

Merrick stopped breathing.

He had watched sharks follow the ship for three days. From the deck they had seemed almost idle, shadows drifting after scraps. Now he could see how large they were. One passed beneath him, its pale underside flashing as it turned.

“I’ll work,” he said. “No share. Until the debt’s paid.”

The captain nodded to the quartermaster.

A sword point touched Merrick between the shoulders.

He took another step. The plank bowed, and his arms flew outward. For one wild instant he thought he might leap backward, catch the rail, drag someone over with him. But the deck was too far away now.

“Please.”

It came out quietly. He hated that more than the trembling.

The sword touched him again.

His foot slipped on the damp wood.

There was a sharp scrape of skin, a cry cut short, and then the sea closed over his head.

He surfaced coughing. The ship towered above him, its rail crowded with faces. He struck out toward it, reaching for a seam in the hull that was yards beyond his grasp.

“Rope!” he shouted. “Throw a—”

Something moved under his legs.

Merrick began swimming harder, wasting his strength in frantic, splashing strokes. A fin rose beside him. He turned toward it, then jerked around as another dark shape approached from behind.

The first impact knocked him sideways.

His scream carried across the still water. He clawed at the surface, vanished, and came up again with his mouth open, struggling to draw enough breath to call out. A red stain spread beneath him.

On deck, Jonah seized a coil of rope.

The quartermaster caught his wrist.

Below them the water erupted. A tail lashed white foam against the hull; a broad gray back rolled through the spreading red. Merrick’s hand appeared once, fingers stretched toward the ship, before a rush of bodies and spray concealed it.

Then the splashing moved away.

Jonah stood holding the rope long after there was anyone left to throw it to.

Captain Vale looked along the rail.

“Back to your stations.”

The men obeyed, slowly at first. Someone hauled the plank aboard. Its wet end struck the deck with a hollow knock, and Finch flinched.

The first night after he killed his brother, Thomas heard someone coughing in the kitchen.

It was a small, polite cough—the kind Daniel used when he wanted your attention but hated to ask for it.

Thomas lay still until morning.

In daylight, the kitchen was empty. The tap dripped. Beneath it, a brown leaf clung to the porcelain sink.

He lived on the seventh floor.

***

For three days he told himself the leaf had come in on his shoe.

For three nights the coughing continued.

He slept with the television on, then with every light on, then not at all. Whenever his eyes closed, he felt the river enter his own mouth: the cold shock, the mud against his tongue, the terrible little bubbles that had risen between his fingers while he held Daniel under.

He had expected a struggle.

He had not expected his brother to keep trying to take his hand.

On the fourth morning, Thomas found wet fingerprints on the inside of his bedroom door.

He wiped them away before examining them closely. Afterward, this seemed a dreadful mistake.

***

The police called on Thursday.

They wanted to know whether Daniel had sounded depressed.

Thomas stood in the hallway with the phone pressed so hard against his ear that the plastic hurt.

“No,” he said.

From the kitchen came a cough.

“Mr. Vale?”

“I don’t know. Maybe.”

Water began creeping beneath the kitchen door.

It advanced slowly across the floorboards, carrying a pale strand of weed.

“Take your time,” the officer said.

Thomas watched the water reach his bare feet.

“He owed people money,” he whispered.

Something moved behind the door. A chair scraped back.

“Other people,” Thomas added.

The officer asked him another question, but he could no longer hear it. The kitchen handle was turning.

He dropped the phone.

When he looked down, the floor was dry.

***

He stopped using the kitchen.

He ordered food and ate it on the landing, where there were footsteps, voices, the elevator’s dependable mechanical groan. Other people could still walk from one room to another without listening first.

His neighbor found him there at two in the morning, holding an unopened sandwich.

“Are you all right?”

Thomas looked at her slippers.

Dry.

“Yes.”

“Someone’s running water in your flat.”

“No.”

“I can hear it.”

He began to cry so suddenly that she stepped back.

***

By Sunday, Daniel was appearing in reflective surfaces.

Not whole. Never conveniently whole.

A shoulder in the dark television. Wet hair beside Thomas’s face in a spoon. Fingers resting on his own shoulder in the bathroom mirror, though he felt nothing until he turned away.

Then the pressure came.

Five cold points.

Thomas smashed the mirror with a shoe. Behind the glass was ordinary plaster, which he also broke, because for one moment he had seen an eye looking through it.

He dug until his nails tore.

Inside the wall, a pipe knocked.

Three times.

Daniel had knocked three times on Thomas’s door that evening.

*Can we talk?*

Such a harmless thing to have said. Thomas tried substituting other words, lying on the floor beside the broken plaster. Accusations. Threats. Anything that might have justified the drive to the river.

But Daniel had only asked to talk.

***

The confession began as practice.

“I pushed him.”

Thomas said it into his phone without dialing.

Then: “I held him down.”

That was harder. He had to stop afterward and breathe.

“I knew he was still alive.”

Behind him, the couch cushions compressed.

Thomas kept his eyes on the blank screen.

“I could have let go.”

The couch springs creaked as something leaned forward.

For the first time in nine days, his apartment became completely quiet.

No dripping. No coughing.

Thomas turned.

His brother sat at the far end of the couch in the clothes he had been wearing when he died. River mud had dried along his jaw. His eyes were open, and Thomas recognized with a sickening intimacy the expression in them: Daniel waiting for him to finish, trying not to interrupt.

“I’m sorry,” Thomas said.

Daniel opened his mouth.

Thomas covered his ears before the water came out.

***

When the police forced the door, they found Thomas kneeling beside the bathtub.

It was empty.

His sleeves were soaked with sweat. Both arms were extended over the porcelain, his hands locked around something they could not see.

They told him to stand.

He shook his head.

They tried to pull him away, and he screamed with such terror that one officer loosened his grip.

“He’s coming up,” Thomas said.

His hands tightened.

“Please. If I let go, he’s coming up.”

The city had been rotting for years. Tonight somebody had peeled back a little skin.

He lay beneath the kitchen window, where the rain worked its way through a cracked frame and collected beside his hand. His throat was a dark, ruined seam. Blood had dried across the linoleum, black in the corners, almost respectable from a distance. Most things in this town were.

I kept my eyes on his face. That was part of the job nobody put on the application: finding the person before the room reduced him to evidence.

Forty, maybe. Cheap haircut. A nick under his chin from a razor that hadn’t known what was coming. He’d shaved this morning. Looked in a mirror, worried about looking presentable. Now one shoe had come off, and I couldn’t stop thinking he would have hated that.

Outside, a streetcar screamed around the bend. The city clearing its throat. Upstairs, somebody turned a radio louder.

There were two cups on the table. Coffee in both. One had a crescent of pale sediment around the bottom, like the scum the river left on its pilings. The other was still half full.

He’d let somebody sit down.

I looked at the overturned chair, the gouges in the table edge. Whatever passed between them, he hadn’t understood it until understanding couldn’t help.

A fly worried the window.

I wanted a cigarette. I wanted the patrolman behind me to quit breathing through his mouth. Mostly, I wanted to go back ten minutes and meet this man as a stranger.

Instead I took out my notebook.

The paper was clean. That never lasted.

Mara spent forty of hers helping a boy climb the fence behind the ration depot. He couldn’t have been more than twelve. One of his shoes had come off in the crush at the release gate.

“Don’t follow the lights,” she told him. “They turn them on so the cameras can see.”

He dropped into the dark beyond the fence.

At ninety seconds, the sirens stopped.

That was worse.

Mara ran through the old financial district, past buildings whose upper floors had disappeared into permanent cloud. Above her, advertising screens woke one by one.

**TONIGHT’S PURSUIT IS BROUGHT TO YOU BY VITALIS.  
A BETTER CLASS OF LIFE.**

Her face appeared beneath the slogan. The photograph was nine years old, taken when she still had a job and an address.

**RUNNER 43.  
THEFT OF MUNICIPAL WATER.  
DEPENDENTS: ONE.**

She ducked into a tram station.

No trains had stopped there for twenty years, but someone had kept sweeping the platform. Small piles of dust stood beside the pillars. Near the ticket booth, a blanket lay neatly folded.

People lived everywhere the city had forgotten to forbid.

A soft chime sounded overhead.

“Runner Forty-Three,” said a pleasant voice. “You have entered a premium viewing zone.”

She looked up.

A camera unfolded from the ceiling.

Mara threw her shoe at it and ran down the tracks.

The hunter caught her at the maintenance gate.

He did not emerge dramatically. He was simply there when she rounded the bend: a man in pale sporting armor, breathing a little heavily, with a silver net-gun braced against his shoulder.

She turned.

The net struck her legs and tightened. Her shoulder hit the concrete. Before she could pull herself upright, he had crossed the distance and pinned the mesh beneath one boot.

“Stay still,” he said. “It’s over.”

He sounded irritated, as though she had continued arguing after a price was agreed.

A drone descended between them, its light settling on her face.

“Verified capture,” it announced. “Contestant Adrian Voss. Elapsed time: eleven minutes, eight seconds.”

Voss lifted his visor. He was younger than Mara had expected. There was a red mark on his forehead where the padding rubbed.

“Alive bonus?” he asked.

“Confirmed.”

Mara pulled once at the net. It tightened around her wrist.

“My daughter,” she said.

He glanced at the drone.

“Do I have to stay for processing?”

“No, Mr. Voss.”

Mara tried again. “There’s a girl at the south ration depot. She’ll be waiting—”

The drone increased the volume of its music.

A compartment opened in its underside. Inside lay a narrow gold pin shaped like a running figure.

Voss took it and fastened it to his chest beside three others. Then he held out his wrist for the credit transfer.

The device chimed.

For the official photograph, he rested one boot on the captured net and smiled.

Mara turned her face toward the tracks. Somewhere beyond the station, the boy was still running. She hoped he had remembered about the lights.

“Look here, please,” the drone told her.

When she didn’t, it took the photograph anyway.

The rain had stopped, but everything kept dripping.

Water fell from the duckboards, from the sandbags, from the cuff of Private Bell’s greatcoat as he held his cigarette beneath his chin. Somewhere beyond the traverse, a man was trying to cough quietly. Bell listened to him fail.

He had just struck a match when the bombardment began.

The first shell lifted the trench floor beneath his boots. The second put out the candle in the dugout. Then there was no counting—only earth hammering his helmet and the terrible pressure of each explosion arriving before its sound.

When it stopped, Bell was on his knees.

His rifle lay beneath a fallen section of revetment. He pulled at the sling. Nothing moved.

A whistle sounded beyond the parapet.

He pulled harder.

Then someone dropped into the trench beside him.

For a moment they simply stared.

The German was young and soaked through, with a pale line beneath his nose where he had wiped away the mud. His rifle was too long for the space between them. He tried to bring it round; the bayonet scraped the timber beside Bell’s ear.

Bell caught the barrel.

They struggled without speaking. The German shoved him against the trench wall, knocking the breath from him. Bell smelled wet wool, tobacco, another man’s breath. He tried to shout, but managed only a grunt.

The rifle went between their boots. Both reached for it. Their helmets struck together with a ridiculous kitchen-clatter sound.

Bell’s hand closed instead on the handle of his trench shovel.

He swung it badly, cramped by the narrow walls. The blade struck the German’s shoulder, and the man cried out. He kept coming. His fingers caught Bell’s collar and twisted until the cloth tightened across his throat.

Bell struck again.

This time the grip loosened.

The German fell against him rather than away, dragging them both into the mud. Bell scrambled upright, slipping on the boards. The other man moved, reaching toward him—or toward the rifle.

Later, Bell would not know which.

He brought the shovel down once more.

Afterward, he stood with it raised.

There was shouting farther along the trench. A rifle fired twice. Someone yelled for bombs. Bell heard all of it distinctly, yet could not make himself turn.

The German lay at his feet with one knee drawn up. His mouth was slightly open. Bell waited for him to move again.

“Stay down,” he said.

The words came out in the voice he used with nervous horses.

He lowered the shovel a little.

“Stay down.”

Blood was running over Bell’s knuckles. He inspected them carefully, searching for a cut. There was a small tear beside his thumbnail, but it could not account for all of it.

He wiped his hand against his coat. Then he wiped it again.

The German’s cap had fallen near the sump. Bell found himself wanting to pick it up. It seemed wrong to leave it there in the dirty water, though the man himself was lying in worse. The thought embarrassed him so sharply that he glanced around to see whether anyone had noticed.

Sergeant Ames came round the traverse.

“Bell. You hurt?”

Bell shook his head.

“Get your rifle.”

He looked at the buried weapon. He understood the order, but could not remember how he had meant to free it.

Ames took the shovel from him. Bell resisted for an instant, his fingers locked around the handle.

“Let go.”

He did.

As Ames levered the timber aside, Bell bent over and vomited into the sump. There was almost nothing in his stomach. Each spasm hurt his throat where the collar had tightened.

His rifle was pushed into his hands.

“Watch the corner.”

Bell went to the corner and knelt. He checked the bolt because his hands knew how. Then he sighted along the trench.

Behind him, Ames stepped over the body.

Bell flinched at the sound of the boot coming down.

In the Commonwealth, the government called executions *corrections*. They took place at noon, between the weather report and the market prices, and attendance counted toward a household’s civic standing.

The crimes were usually small. Small crimes, the ministers explained, revealed large defects before they had time to spread.

***

The boy’s name was Tomas Vale. He was sixteen. The clerk announced both facts in the same voice he used to announce the date.

Around the square, people kept their faces arranged.

Mara had learned the proper expression from a poster at the tram stop: attentive, sober, neither cruel nor weak. She wore it now with her hands clasped around the strap of her shopping bag.

On the platform stood a table. On the table lay the loaf of bread.

Someone had placed it on a white cloth.

“That’s not even a whole one,” said a little girl nearby.

Her father bent so quickly that his hat fell off. He whispered into her ear, then straightened without retrieving it.

The clerk read the charge. Theft from a licensed bakery. Attempted flight. Deprivation of lawful revenue. Tomas watched a pigeon walking beneath the front row of chairs.

The chairs were reserved for exemplary citizens. Nobody sitting in them moved.

Mara remembered seeing the boy in the baker’s doorway three days earlier. She had remembered him all morning, although she kept telling herself there was no reason to be certain. Plenty of boys wore coats too short at the wrists.

“The accused was offered an opportunity to explain his conduct,” the clerk said.

Tomas looked up.

“I said—”

The clerk continued reading.

A woman near the fountain made a small sound. Everyone around her shifted away, not far enough to be obvious, but enough that she suddenly stood in a little clearing of her own. An officer turned toward her. She covered her mouth and coughed.

Several people coughed with her.

Mara stared at the white cloth. The loaf had split along its top in the oven, making a brown ridge. She wondered who would have to collect it afterward. Then she hated herself for wondering something so ordinary.

The clerk folded his paper.

The crowd knew the sequence. Hats off. Heads forward. No closing of eyes: the cameras above the pharmacy had been upgraded in spring.

Tomas searched the square. His gaze moved from face to face with an urgency that made Mara want to step behind the man beside her.

She stayed where she was.

The guards positioned the boy beside the table. At the signal, a single shot sounded across the square, and Tomas fell out of Mara’s sight behind the platform rail.

The pigeon lifted away.

For a moment nobody applauded.

That was the dangerous moment, the interval afterward. Mara heard the fountain splashing. Somewhere behind her, a person was breathing in short, uneven pulls.

Then the bakery owner began to clap.

He stood in the front row, his apron wound tightly between his hands. He had to unwind it before he could bring his palms together. His face was wet.

Others joined him. Unevenly at first, then all at once.

Mara clapped too. She watched the baker, who was looking at the loaf rather than at the guards carrying the boy away.

When the loudspeakers released them, the crowd moved toward the tram stops and shopping streets. The little girl’s father picked up his hat. The woman by the fountain remained where she was until an officer told her to go home.

At the bakery, a queue formed before the owner had returned to unlock the door.

Mara joined it. She still had to feed her children.

When her turn came, she asked for two loaves. The baker put them on the counter, and neither of them could look at the other while she counted out the money.

“Close the doors.

“Not because you are prisoners. Have I ever called you prisoners?

“No. Leave them open, then. If the sight of an open door is what you need to trust me, leave them open.

“For twenty years, you have asked me what waits beyond this world. I gave you words large enough to live inside. *Ascension. Deliverance. Home.*

“Why are you looking at me like that?

“Yes, Daniel. I heard your question.

“You want to know whether I’ve seen it.

“I have stood before you every morning. I have buried your parents. I have given your children their names. And now, tonight, you demand—

“No. Stay where you are. Please.

“I thought certainty was something a man could build. Say a thing often enough, say it without trembling, and one day there would be something beneath it. Something solid.

“But you kept believing me.

“Every year, you believed me more. And every year, it became harder to tell you that I was still waiting for the first sign.

“Don’t ask me to make the waiting mean something now.

“There is no sign.

“There is only this room, and what I nearly asked you to do.

“Leave the doors open.”

The bathroom door resisted at first, its lower edge swollen against the frame. When she pushed it open, the smell reached her before she saw the tub.

It was not simply the odor of something rotten. There was a thick sweetness to it, like spoiled fruit sealed in a hot cupboard, beneath which lay the sulfurous stink of sewage and a sharp ammonia note that caught in her nose. She gagged and stepped back. Breathing through her mouth only made it seem to settle on her tongue.

The body lay partly submerged in cloudy, discolored water. In the warmth of the closed bathroom, a week had altered it almost beyond recognition. The abdomen was distended with gas; the face looked swollen, its familiar angles lost. Across the exposed skin, dull green discoloration darkened toward purple. Branching, veinlike patterns showed beneath the surface.

One hand rested against the side of the tub. The fingertips were pale and deeply wrinkled, the skin waterlogged and softened. Around the wrist, the outer layer had begun to loosen. Elsewhere, small blisters interrupted the skin, and patches had slipped away where the body pressed against the porcelain. A dark stain marked the corner of the mouth.

She fixed her eyes on the faucet instead. A bead of water gathered there, trembled, and dropped.

The smell had filled the room so completely that nothing seemed separate from it—not the damp towels, the bathmat, the half-open bottle of shampoo. Each breath brought the same dense mixture, sweet at first and then foul enough to make her stomach contract. She pressed her sleeve over her nose, but the fabric offered almost no relief.

Backing into the hall, she took a breath she expected to be clean. It wasn’t. The odor had followed her through the open doorway. She fumbled for her phone, eyes watering, unable for a moment to remember how to unlock it.

The collector laid the receipt on the kitchen table and smoothed it with two fingers.

“Friday,” he said.

“I know.”

“It’s Monday.”

Rain ticked against the window. Somewhere upstairs, a television audience laughed.

Martin stared at the baseball bat hanging beside the collector’s coat. The barrel was scuffed white.

“I’ve got half,” Martin said. “In the cupboard. You can take it.”

The collector looked toward the cupboard, then back at him.

Martin tried to get past him. His sock slipped on the linoleum, and he caught the edge of the table hard enough to spill yesterday’s coffee.

The bat struck with a heavy thud.

His scream startled him. It was too loud for the little kitchen, too loud to belong to him. He dropped beneath the table, dragging a chair down with him, and held both hands out.

“Wait. Please, wait.”

The collector pulled the chair aside.

The second blow broke his other leg.

For a moment Martin couldn’t make a sound. His mouth stayed open while he fought for breath. Then he began calling for his brother, who lived two hundred miles away.

The collector opened the cupboard. Coins rattled into a biscuit tin.

“Does this count?” Martin whispered.

The collector paused.

“The money. Does it count toward—”

“Yes.”

After the door closed, Martin lay listening to the refrigerator hum. His phone was on the counter. He could see the charging cable dangling over the edge, just beyond his reach.

The forest went quiet by degrees.

First the frogs stopped. Then the small things in the brush. At last there was only the wind high in the pines, moving through branches Mara could not see.

She stood on the trail with her phone raised.

No signal.

Behind her, somewhere beyond the reach of the screen’s pale light, a twig broke.

“Hello?”

He closed his eyes when she said it.

There it was: the little courtesy people offered the dark. As if whatever waited inside it might be embarrassed to have caused alarm.

He had heard the word before. Different voices, different nights. Sometimes impatient. Sometimes already trembling.

Mara lowered the phone. Its light had shown her almost nothing, but now that it was gone, the trees seemed closer.

“If somebody’s there, I’m calling the police.”

He disliked this part—not the threat, but the way people said things they both knew were untrue. He had spent most of his life being lied to politely. At work, in shops, across dinner tables. Faces turned toward him while attention wandered elsewhere.

Out here, she was listening to him.

That was what he enjoyed. Not simply being feared, though he had once told himself that was enough. He enjoyed occupying every thought in another person’s mind. She would not be thinking about tomorrow’s errands now. Whatever argument she’d had, whatever small disappointment had followed her into the woods, he had replaced it.

He eased his weight from one foot to the other.

Mara turned toward the sound.

He smiled before he could help himself, then felt foolish. There was nobody to see it.

“Daniel?” she called.

The name irritated him.

For a moment he imagined answering, letting her relief carry her toward him. But the voice she wanted belonged to someone with a history he did not know, and he resented that history: the familiar jokes, the ordinary afternoons, all the unremarkable ways this Daniel had been allowed close.

Mara waited.

Then she began walking.

He followed.

The trail curved downhill through a stand of firs. She stumbled once and caught herself against a trunk. He heard her breathing change. When she resumed walking, her steps came faster.

He knew the pattern from the others. The effort to remain sensible. The reluctance to run before there was something definite to run from. Later, he would remember these small hesitations with a clarity that made the rest of his days seem dim.

A branch scraped his coat.

Mara stopped again.

This time she did not call out.

He found her silence less satisfying than he had expected.

Through the trees, far below, a pair of headlights moved along the road. She saw them too. Her phone flashed on, illuminating her hand and the white curve of her jaw.

“Please,” she whispered at the screen.

The word was not for him.

He stepped forward.

She ran.

For several seconds the woods were full of her: shoes striking roots, brush snapping back, a sharp breath when she fell. He moved after the noise, feeling the familiar lift in his chest.

Then a phone began ringing.

He stopped.

It was not hers.

The sound came from his coat pocket, absurdly cheerful in the dark. He fumbled for it, furious, and saw his sister’s name.

By the time he silenced it, Mara’s footsteps had disappeared.

He listened.

Wind passed through the pines. Somewhere downhill, a car horn sounded, long and insistent.

He stood with the phone warm in his palm, waiting for the forest to give her back.

I wake to the smell before I open my eyes.

Old blood—coppery, stale—mingles with the damp mineral breath of the walls. Underneath it is rust, wet leather, and the sourness of a room that has been shut too long. I try breathing through my mouth. It doesn’t help.

A lamp hangs above a wooden table, its light trembling each time something moves in the ceiling. Pipes, perhaps. I listen for another sound and hear water dripping somewhere behind me.

My wrists are fastened to the arms of a chair.

For a while, I look only at the buckles. The leather is dark and polished along its edges. One strap has been repaired with neat, pale stitches. Someone has taken the trouble to mend it.

Beyond my knees stands a trolley. Pliers. Narrow blades. A heavy instrument whose purpose I cannot understand and do not want to. Everything rests on a cloth that might once have been white.

Hooks project from the far wall. Chains hang beneath them, some ending just above the floor. There is a drain under the table, set into a shallow depression in the stone.

I search for a window.

There isn’t one.

Beside the door, a coat hangs from a peg. Beneath it sit a pair of ordinary shoes, carefully aligned. Their presence frightens me more than the chains. Whoever comes here changes their shoes. Hangs up their coat. Then turns toward this chair.

Footsteps sound outside.

I close my eyes before I can decide whether pretending to sleep will help.

The first thing that went wrong was the door.

It should have opened onto the alley. Eddie had checked it twice, once dressed as a courier, once as a man looking for the restroom. But now there was a new steel bar across it, bright enough to catch the emergency lights.

He shoved it anyway.

Behind him, inside First County Savings, the alarm kept screaming.

“Tell me,” Mara said.

Eddie turned. His mask had slipped below his nose. “We’re not going out this way.”

For a moment she heard nothing—not the alarm, not the teller crying beneath her desk, not Cal telling everyone to keep their heads down. All morning she had been counting backward from this moment: alley, car, highway, gone.

Now there was nowhere left to count.

Red and blue light washed across the frosted front windows.

Cal saw it and raised his rifle.

“No,” Mara said.

He fired before she could reach him.

The lobby windows burst outward in a glittering sheet. The rifle’s report struck the marble walls and came back multiplied, a hard, concussive roar that seemed too large for the room. Someone screamed. The security guard curled around his own head.

Outside, a police officer staggered against the hood of his cruiser. His partner caught his sleeve, lost it, then dragged him down behind the engine block. One of his shoes remained visible beneath the car, rocking once before it stopped.

“Cal!” Mara grabbed his shoulder.

He twisted away, firing again.

The police answered.

Glass jumped from the teller partitions. A brass lamp snapped sideways. Bullets punched pale wounds in the stone column beside Mara’s face, showering her with grit. She dropped behind a desk so hard her teeth clicked together.

Eddie was still standing in the corridor.

“Get down!”

He looked at her, confused, as though she had asked him a question in another language.

Then his shirt jerked at the chest.

He sat down abruptly against the wall. The bag of money slipped from his hand and spilled open beside him. Bundles slid across the polished floor.

Mara crawled to him.

“Stay with me.”

Eddie pressed both hands against his shirt. Blood pushed between his fingers and darkened the cuffs.

“It doesn’t hurt,” he said, frightened by that.

She pulled his hands aside and leaned her weight onto the wound. He gasped and seized her wrist.

Across the lobby, Cal crouched behind the stone deposit counter. Each time he rose, the muzzle flashed white-orange in the dusty air. Each time he ducked, police rounds cracked over him and struck the wall of brochures.

A leaflet drifted down beside Eddie’s shoe.

*Plan for tomorrow.*

His grip loosened.

“Look at me,” Mara said.

He tried. His eyes found her face, slipped away, found it again.

She had known him since he was sixteen. He used to steal oranges from the market and leave half on her doorstep.

“Eddie.”

His mouth moved without sound.

Then his hand fell.

Mara stayed bent over him until another burst tore through the desk behind her.

At the front doors, an officer appeared low behind a shield, pulling the wounded security guard toward the entrance. Cal rose and fired twice.

The officer dropped to one knee. The shield struck the floor with a flat metallic crash. Outside, someone shouted his name.

The guard crawled the last few feet alone.

“Stop shooting!” Mara screamed.

Cal turned toward her. His mask was gone. He looked sick and astonished.

“They’re shooting at us!”

“You started it!”

He glanced toward Eddie.

That brief look cost him.

The next volley hit the counter, the wall, and Cal. He pitched backward, rifle clattering across the marble. One foot scraped against the floor as he tried to get underneath himself. Then he lay still, blood spreading beneath his coat.

The gunfire stopped in pieces.

First the long bursts. Then two isolated shots. Then only the alarm, the ringing in Mara’s ears, and a man outside pleading, “Come on, stay awake.”

She took her pistol out slowly and laid it beside Eddie. She had never fired it.

“I’m putting it down!” she shouted. “I’m coming out!”

She crossed the lobby on her knees, hands raised. Glass cut through her trousers. At the doors she could see the officer beside the cruiser, his partner pressing down on his chest with straight, desperate arms. Nearer the entrance, another officer lay beneath a darkening dressing while a medic worked over him.

“Face down!” someone ordered.

Mara lowered herself onto the pavement. It was warm from the afternoon sun.

Hands wrenched her arms behind her. A cuff closed over Eddie’s blood on her wrist.

Through the broken doorway, the money lay where it had fallen. A loose bill stirred in the breeze, caught against his shoe, and stayed there.

At first, Mara thought the hiss came from the pipes.

Then her eyes began to burn.

She crossed to the door and pulled the handle. It stopped halfway down. She tried again, harder, bracing one foot against the frame.

“Hello?”

The room gave her voice back, small and flat.

She noticed the vent above the door. A faint stream stirred the dust caught along its grille. She dragged a chair beneath it, climbed, and pressed her sleeves against the openings, but the air slipped around her hands. Her first cough nearly knocked her off balance.

“Somebody open the door!”

She jumped down and hammered with both fists. Between blows she listened for footsteps. The hiss continued.

Her throat felt scraped raw. She tried to take a deep breath and couldn’t finish it; a painful tightening in her chest stopped her short. She coughed until tears ran down her face, then bent over, waiting for the next breath to come.

There had to be something she hadn’t tried.

She searched her pockets again. Empty. Looked beneath the table again. Nothing. She couldn’t remember why she’d thought something might be there.

The handle blurred when she reached for it. Her fingertips missed, scraped the door, found it at last. She pulled with both hands now, though some distant part of her knew pulling wasn’t the problem.

Her knees folded.

For a moment she stayed upright by hanging from the handle. Then her grip loosened and she slid down the door, one shoe squeaking against the floor.

She meant to shout. What came out was a hoarse, breathless sound.

Lying on her side, she watched the chair beside the vent. She ought to move it. Stand on it. Try something.

Her hand shifted an inch across the floor.

Then it stopped.

At first, Mara thought the hiss came from the pipes.

Then her eyes began to burn.

She crossed to the door and pulled the handle. It stopped halfway down. She tried again, harder, bracing one foot against the frame.

“Hello?”

The room gave her voice back, small and flat.

She noticed the vent above the door. A faint stream stirred the dust caught along its grille. She dragged a chair beneath it, climbed, and pressed her sleeves against the openings, but the air slipped around her hands. Her first cough nearly knocked her off balance.

“Somebody open the door!”

She jumped down and hammered with both fists. Between blows she listened for footsteps. The hiss continued.

Her throat felt scraped raw. She tried to take a deep breath and couldn’t finish it; a painful tightening in her chest stopped her short. She coughed until tears ran down her face, then bent over, waiting for the next breath to come.

There had to be something she hadn’t tried.

She searched her pockets again. Empty. Looked beneath the table again. Nothing. She couldn’t remember why she’d thought something might be there.

The handle blurred when she reached for it. Her fingertips missed, scraped the door, found it at last. She pulled with both hands now, though some distant part of her knew pulling wasn’t the problem.

Her knees folded.

For a moment she stayed upright by hanging from the handle. Then her grip loosened and she slid down the door, one shoe squeaking against the floor.

She meant to shout. What came out was a hoarse, breathless sound.

Lying on her side, she watched the chair beside the vent. She ought to move it. Stand on it. Try something.

Her hand shifted an inch across the floor.

Then it stopped.

results.model_response:
Officer Vale waited until the ambulance doors closed before he decided who would be guilty.

Not the woman from the bakery. Too many people knew her. Not the delivery driver, either; the camera above his windshield had a blinking blue light.

The young man sitting on the curb would do.

His name was Daniel Mercer. Vale had taken his statement ten minutes earlier: twenty-six, warehouse worker, walking home because his car was in the shop. He had found the jeweler bleeding behind the store and called for help.

He was still watching the ambulance.

“Is he going to make it?” Daniel asked.

Vale looked down at his notebook. He had written *witness* beside Daniel’s name.

“We’ll find out.”

The jeweler had recognized Vale despite the cap, despite the hour. Had said his name with the relief of a man expecting rescue.

Then he had noticed the gun.

Vale pressed the pen hard enough to leave a groove through three pages. He crossed out *witness*.

“Stand up for me, Daniel.”

Daniel rose stiffly. There was blood on one cuff where he had tried to hold the wound closed. Vale considered that useful, though not sufficient.

“What’s going on?”

“Just clearing up a few things.”

Vale guided him toward the patrol car with a hand on his elbow. Not a grip. A grip invited resistance, and resistance would draw attention before Vale was ready for it.

At the car, Daniel pulled out his phone.

“Can I call my wife?”

“In a minute.”

“She’ll be worried.”

Vale held out his hand. After a moment, Daniel gave him the phone.

The screen lit with a photograph of Daniel beside a woman wearing a paper crown in a restaurant. Vale turned it facedown on the roof.

The stolen watch lay in Vale’s coat pocket, wrapped in the jeweler’s polishing cloth. He could feel its weight against his hip. He had chosen it because it was small, because he knew what it was worth, because he had stood in that shop in uniform three weeks earlier while the jeweler showed it to him.

Now it had become a problem with a convenient solution.

“Face the car.”

Daniel obeyed. “Am I under arrest?”

Vale did not answer immediately. He glanced toward his partner, Haskins, who was speaking to the ambulance driver across the street. Then he looked at Daniel’s lowered head.

This was the point at which there was still a choice. Vale recognized it without discomfort, much as he recognized an intersection while driving through it.

He slipped the watch into Daniel’s coat.

A moment later he brought it out again.

“What’s this?”

Daniel turned. Vale pushed him back against the car.

“I don’t know.”

“Keep your hands where they are.”

“I don’t know what that is.”

Vale raised the watch where Haskins could see it.

“Got something.”

Haskins started across the street. Daniel looked from the watch to Vale’s face, waiting for some sign that the confusion was mutual.

There was none.

“You put that there,” he said.

Vale tightened one cuff, then the other. Daniel’s voice had changed, and Vale noted that too. Fear would make him loud. Loud would make Haskins cautious. Once Haskins began giving orders, he would have less attention available for questions.

“What have we got?” Haskins asked.

“Property from the store. In his pocket.”

“No,” Daniel said. “No, he just—”

“Let’s settle down,” Haskins told him.

Vale felt the first small easing in his chest.

He put Daniel in the back seat and closed the door. Through the glass, Daniel was still speaking. Vale could hear the cadence but not the words.

His phone remained on the roof.

It began to ring.

Vale glanced at the name on the screen, then carried it around to the evidence bag on the front seat. He would have paperwork to finish before morning. The statement needed to be clear, restrained, free of unnecessary detail.

He opened his notebook to a clean page.

Behind him, Daniel struck the window once with his bound hands.

Vale wrote the time.

results.model_response:
The cache lay beneath the pharmacy floor: six swollen tins, a split sack of rice, and a jar of peaches gone gray in their syrup.

For a moment, nobody moved.

Rain ticked through the ruined ceiling. Mara knelt beside the open hatch, holding one tin in both hands. Its label had dissolved years ago.

“Share it,” she said.

Dane looked at the seven people crowded around her. Then at the little girl asleep against her mother’s shoulder.

“That won’t feed us.”

“It’s what there is.”

He reached for the sack.

Mara caught his wrist, and someone behind them shouted. The sack split farther as Dane pulled. Rice spilled between the floorboards, pattering into the dark below.

The first blow came from a length of copper pipe.

It caught Dane across the forearm with a dull crack. He dropped the sack and stumbled backward, his hand hanging at an angle that made everyone hesitate—everyone except the man holding the pipe.

He stooped for the food.

Mara struck him with the tin.

After that, there was no room to swing properly. They fought shoulder to shoulder among fallen shelves, slipping on wet paper and spilled rice. A sharpened screwdriver flashed near Mara’s face. She caught the wrist behind it and drove its owner against a cabinet, once, twice, until the screwdriver fell.

Across the hatch, the child’s mother dragged a sack toward the doorway. Someone hooked her ankle with a bent curtain rod. She fell hard without letting go of her daughter. Her head struck the threshold, and she stayed there blinking, trying to rise while the girl began to scream.

“Stop,” Mara said.

Nobody heard her.

Dane lunged past, cradling his broken arm. With his good hand he seized the peach jar. The man with the pipe hit him in the ribs. Dane folded over it, breath leaving him in a thin, helpless whistle.

The jar broke beneath his knees.

They all saw the peaches spread across the filthy floor.

For several seconds, the only sounds were rain and Dane trying to breathe.

Then the man with the pipe knelt and picked one up.

Mara watched him wipe it on his sleeve. His lips were split. He was shaking too badly to bring it to his mouth.

Near the doorway, the mother had managed to sit up. She held out an empty hand.

Mara found an unbroken tin beside her boot. She set it down between them and searched the floor for the screwdriver.

They still needed something to open it.

At six o’clock on an October morning in 1816, Henry Vale discovered that the field chosen for his death was full of sheep.

They watched from the far side of a broken wall while the seconds measured the distance. Their presence struck him as absurd. He had spent the night writing letters in a hand he hoped would look steady, and now there were sheep cropping the grass as though nothing important had been arranged.

Across the field, Captain Rook stood with his coat buttoned to the throat.

“An apology may still be offered,” said Henry’s second.

Henry looked at Rook. The captain looked back. Neither spoke.

The pistols were brought out.

Henry had imagined this moment so often that the actual weight of the weapon surprised him. It was heavier than the pistol in his thoughts, and colder. He settled his forefinger against the trigger.

At the signal, both men raised their arms.

Henry’s shot went into the wall.

Rook’s struck him in the stomach.

For a moment Henry remained standing. He looked down with an expression almost of annoyance, as though someone had spilled wine over his waistcoat. Then his knees folded.

His second caught him badly, and the two of them went down together in the wet grass.

“Don’t move,” the man said.

Henry tried to answer, but a deep, constricting pain had taken hold beneath his ribs. He drew up his legs. That hurt. He straightened them. That hurt worse.

The surgeon knelt beside him, opened his coat, and called for a folded cloth.

“Is it serious?” Henry asked.

The surgeon did not answer quickly enough.

“Oh,” Henry said.

The first minute passed in confusion: hands moving over him, his second asking questions, someone telling Rook to remain where he was. Henry kept trying to lift his head. He wanted to see what they were doing, but each effort tightened the pain until he could think of nothing else.

“Lie still, Mr. Vale.”

“I am trying.”

He said it irritably, and then apologized.

During the second minute, he asked for water. The surgeon wetted his lips with a handkerchief. Henry turned toward it eagerly, disappointed by how little relief it gave.

Captain Rook approached and stopped several paces away.

“Vale,” he said.

Henry shut his eyes.

“Vale, I had no wish—”

“Then you should have missed.”

Nobody spoke after that.

By the third minute, Henry was trembling. The pain came in fierce waves, leaving him only a few shallow breaths between them. He gripped his second’s wrist and held it with surprising strength.

“Charles.”

“I’m here.”

“My letters are in the blue case. Not the black one.”

“Yes.”

“One is unfinished.”

“I’ll see to it.”

“You mustn’t finish it yourself.”

Charles bent his head. “No.”

At four minutes, Henry began asking whether the carriage had come. It stood beyond the gate, plainly visible, but when they tried to move him he cried out and begged them to stop. The surgeon eased him back onto the grass.

For a while Henry could manage only short, strained sounds. Charles took off his own coat and laid it over him, although Henry complained that he was too hot. A few breaths later, he asked for it to be pulled higher.

Rook turned away.

“Stay,” Henry said suddenly.

The captain faced him again.

Henry seemed to have something more to say. His mouth moved, but the words would not come. He swallowed, waited through another spasm, and finally whispered, “Never mind.”

Near the end of the sixth minute, his grip loosened. Charles kept holding his hand.

The surgeon leaned close, listening.

Henry drew one breath that appeared to cost him an immense effort. He waited a long time before taking another.

Then there was only the morning wind.

Rook remained beside them until the surgeon closed his case. Across the wall, one of the sheep lifted its head at the sound of the clasp, then lowered it to the grass again.

The room had been empty long enough for the wallpaper to loosen at the seams.

He set the case on a table beneath a water stain and opened it. Inside, the rifle rested in fitted darkness, its separate pieces as immaculate as instruments laid out before surgery.

He took off his coat.

There was no haste in the preparation. Metal caught the gray window light and lost it again beneath his hands. Small mechanical sounds punctuated the silence: a muted click, the whisper of fabric, a brief scrape against the table. His movements were economical, almost dull. He paused only to fold the empty cloth and place it back in the case.

On the television in the corner, the minister was already arriving.

The sound was off. A reporter spoke beneath a bright banner while people gathered behind barriers, craning to see the motorcade. Someone held a child above the crowd. The child waved a paper flag so vigorously that it tore.

He glanced at the screen, then returned to his work.

The photograph he had been given was several years old. In it, the minister looked younger and heavier, with the confident smile of a man expecting agreement. The man on television looked tired. An aide leaned close to say something, and the minister listened with his eyes lowered.

Neither version interested him.

When the rifle was ready, he settled behind it. The distant scene narrowed to pale stone, dark suits, faces passing briefly through view.

He found the minister.

For a moment, someone stood in the way. He waited, his expression unchanged. Below, applause lifted faintly through the glass.

Then the minister stepped forward.

The crosshairs rested on his head.

He watched the man turn toward the crowd and smile. A hand rose to smooth his hair, an ordinary, slightly vain gesture. He made no effort to imagine the life surrounding it—the breakfast left unfinished, the person expecting a call that evening.

He checked his watch once.

Then he returned his eye to the scope, patient and untroubled, while the minister began to speak.

The motel towel had been white once. Now it lay beneath his thigh, darkening while the bathroom tap dripped steadily into a rust-stained sink.

He had arranged his tools on the nightstand: nail scissors, a pair of bent tweezers, a pocketknife with a loose hinge. Under the yellow lamp they looked less like instruments than things found beneath a car seat. He wiped them again anyway. It gave his hands something to do.

The first touch of metal made him jerk so hard the bed frame struck the wall.

“No,” he whispered. “Stay still.”

Pain crowded everything else out. The television vanished, then the traffic beyond the curtains, then the sentence he had been trying to remember. He found himself gripping the mattress seam with his free hand, unable to loosen his fingers. Sweat ran into his eyes. When he tried again, a small, involuntary sound escaped him—nothing like the noise he had imagined a tough man making.

Blood slicked the tweezers. He set them down before he dropped them.

For a while he could only stare at his leg and breathe through his open mouth. The bullet was somewhere he couldn’t see. Every time he thought he had found it, his hand began to shake.

Someone laughed in the next room.

He looked toward the sound, absurdly offended, then reached for another towel.

“I know about the wire,” Varga said.

He placed a little black transmitter on the table between them.

Adrian looked at it, then at the door. A mistake. Varga noticed everything.

“No one’s coming through there,” the boss said. “But you can keep watching it.”

The room had once been a restaurant office. There were pale rectangles where photographs had hung, a calendar three years out of date, a hook with an apron still on it. Adrian concentrated on the apron. Someone had tied its strings together before hanging it up.

Behind him, a drawer opened.

“Which agency?” Varga asked.

“I don’t know what you think—”

“Don’t spend your first answer on something neither of us believes.”

The man behind Adrian took his left hand and laid it flat on the table. He did this carefully, almost courteously. Adrian tried to pull away, but the restraints stopped him.

Varga watched his face.

There had been training for this: ways to regulate his breathing, ways to prepare a plausible lie, reminders that panic made promises it couldn’t keep. Adrian could remember the instructor’s shirt more clearly than any of the instructions.

“Please,” he said.

It escaped before he could decide what he meant by it.

Varga leaned back. “That isn’t an answer.”

Adrian heard the tool being set down. He kept looking at the apron.

When they took the nail, he lost sight of it.

For several seconds there was only pain. He couldn’t hold a thought long enough to use it. His chair struck the wall, and afterward he realized the sound filling the little office was his own voice.

Then they let go of his hand.

He folded over it as far as the restraints allowed. Each breath came shallow and fast. He wanted to protect the finger, but even the prospect of touching it frightened him.

Varga pushed a glass of water closer.

Adrian stared at the glass. He hated him more for that than for the drawer, the tool, the quiet instruction Adrian hadn’t quite heard.

“Which agency?”

“Federal.”

“Good. Your contact?”

Adrian shut his eyes.

A hand settled on his shoulder. Nothing more. He flinched so hard that fresh pain went through him.

“The name,” Varga said.

“Mercer.”

Varga studied him for a moment, then opened a folder.

Inside was a photograph of Mercer entering Adrian’s apartment building. Beneath it was another photograph: Adrian at a courthouse, years before, standing beside a man Varga had ordered him to kill.

Varga tapped that one.

“You told me he was dead.”

Adrian’s mouth had gone dry. “He is.”

“He testified yesterday.”

Outside the office, someone laughed. Plates clattered. The restaurant was still open.

Varga closed the folder and glanced at the man behind Adrian.

“Now,” he said, “we can stop discussing who you work for.”

Adrian watched the drawer.

“We can discuss how long.”

The vats sang in E-flat.

That was what Mara noticed on her first night beneath the city, before she learned not to notice anything. Six ceramic cylinders stood behind reinforced glass, their heaters humming in a harmony too steady to be accidental.

“Helps the equipment last,” her predecessor had told her.

“The sound?”

“The steady temperature.”

He retired eleven days later. Someone else handled it.

Now Mara wore his apron.

Above her, New Carthage glittered through another manufactured winter. Snow fell in the financial district between six and nine each evening. Here, beneath the municipal reclamation plant, condensation gathered on the ceiling and dropped into buckets nobody had emptied in years.

A delivery arrived at 02:13.

Mara heard the freight lift settle, then the scrape of something heavy across its floor. Two men stepped out with a sealed transport shroud between them. One was new. She could tell because he looked at the vats.

The other held out a payment wafer.

“Priority.”

“Everything’s priority.”

“This one actually is.”

She placed the wafer against the reader. The account flashed green.

The older courier left immediately. The new one lingered, staring at the long shape on the trolley.

“Does it really just—”

“Yes,” Mara said.

He waited for more. She watched him until he went back into the lift.

There had once been a proper sequence to the work: verify the manifest, inspect the containment seals, record the delivery. Then the city privatized reclamation, and the new owners discovered that records were a needless expense.

Now the screen asked three questions.

**RECEIPT CONFIRMED?**

Mara pressed yes.

**ORGANIC LOAD?**

Yes.

**AUTHORIZED PROCESSING?**

She touched the payment reader again.

The trolley traveled into the chamber on its recessed track. Beyond the glass, an articulated frame lifted the shroud and lowered it into an empty cradle above the nearest vat. Its joints moved with the careful hesitation of an elderly person sitting down.

Mara checked the green indicators. She did not check inside the shroud.

She had stopped doing that in her third year.

The chamber shutter descended before the cradle tipped. There was a muted mechanical sound, then a change in the pumps’ pitch. Acid circulated somewhere behind the glass and steel. The old control system displayed pressure, temperature, and a reassuring animation of a blue leaf.

Occasionally a seal failed and the ventilation caught a sharp chemical smell before it reached her station. Usually there was nothing. The chamber was designed to make dangerous work uneventful.

Mara sat down with her tea.

When the cycle finished, the machinery would transfer what remained to another closed system. Eventually she would receive an empty cradle, a clean trolley, and a line of text telling her the room was ready again.

She used to watch the progress bar. Now she watched a cooking program with the sound off.

Onscreen, a woman folded dough around something golden. Mara had seen this episode four times. She liked the woman’s hands. They always knew what to do next.

Halfway through the cycle, her terminal chimed.

**UNDECLARED PERSONAL EFFECT DETECTED.**

“Of course,” she said.

A small compartment opened beside the console. Inside lay a plastic bracelet recovered by the intake sorter.

Cheap yellow beads. Stretch cord. The sort children made in supervised recreation hours.

The beads spelled **DAD**.

Mara held it between two fingers.

For a moment she felt the familiar irritation of finding a coin in a machine filter. Someone had been careless. The courier should have cleared the delivery. Now she would have to dispose of it separately.

Then she read the beads again.

She waited.

Years ago, something like this would have spoiled her tea. She might have gone home and stood in the shower, rehearsing a conversation in which she quit. She had rehearsed that conversation often enough to know both sides.

But her tea still tasted pleasantly bitter. Her back still ached. She was still mildly annoyed that the bracelet had interrupted the program.

That frightened her enough to make her put it down.

The vat stopped humming.

**PROCESSING COMPLETE.**

Mara cleared the notification.

On the silent television, the woman lifted her finished pastry toward the camera. Steam rose around her fingers.

The freight lift chimed upstairs. Another delivery.

Mara stood, tightened the apron at her waist, and reached for the drawer where she kept confiscated watches, rings, and loose change.

She paused with the bracelet over it.

Then she put it in her pocket.

She did not know whether this was kindness, theft, or merely a new habit. There was no time to decide. The lift doors were opening, and someone was already saying they were in a hurry.

“He saw you.”

“He saw both of us.”

“Then why am I the only one thinking clearly?”

Mara stood beside the service door, still wearing her gloves. On the other side of it, a chair scraped once against concrete.

Ellis glanced toward the sound. “Keep your voice down.”

“What’s he going to do, complain?”

“You’re enjoying this too much.”

“I’m not enjoying any of it. I told you to leave him behind.”

“He was standing in the doorway.”

“And you brought him through it.”

Ellis rubbed at the red mark his mask had left across his forehead. Mara watched him do it.

“He keeps looking at me,” she said.

“He’s scared.”

“He’s remembering.”

“You don’t know what he’s doing.”

“I know what I’d be doing.”

For a moment, neither spoke. Water ticked into a bucket somewhere in the building.

Mara held out her hand. “Give it here.”

“No.”

“Then do it yourself.”

“No.”

“You’ve said that twice. It isn’t a plan.”

Ellis looked down at the gun in his hand, as though she had only just made him aware of it. He put it inside his coat.

Mara’s hand remained out.

“You getting decent on me?” she asked.

“Don’t be stupid.”

“That’s what it looks like.”

“I didn’t say let him go. I said stop.”

“Stop until when?”

He had no answer ready. She saw that, too.

Behind the door, the hostage coughed.

Mara lowered her hand. “You talked to him.”

“He talked to me.”

“What did he tell you?”

“Nothing.”

“A name?”

Ellis stared at her.

“There it is,” she said.

“It doesn’t change anything.”

“Then tell me his name.”

“Leave it.”

“Tell me.”

Ellis stepped between her and the door.

Mara looked at his coat, then at his face. Her voice became quieter.

“We’ve worked together nine years.”

“I know.”

“I need to know which side of that door you’re on.”

He swallowed. “This side.”

“Move, then.”

He didn’t.

The chair scraped again.

Mara took one slow step back, putting space between them. That frightened Ellis more than when she had held out her hand.

“All right,” she said. “Now we’ve got two problems.”

The alley was too narrow to fall cleanly.

When Mara’s legs buckled, her shoulder struck the brick wall and kept her upright. Someone in the ring of spectators laughed. Someone else shouted odds she couldn’t make out over the ringing in her ears.

“Hands up,” her corner man said.

She tried.

The next punch struck above her left eye with a hard, flat crack. Light flashed across her vision. Her head snapped sideways, and for a moment the alley seemed to tilt—the fire escape overhead, the yellow bulb above the service door, the wet pavement under her shoes.

She brought her gloves up out of habit.

No gloves. Just fists. She had forgotten that for a second.

Her opponent stepped closer.

Mara caught the first body shot against her elbow. The second landed beneath it, driving the breath out of her in a small, humiliating grunt. She folded forward and took a knuckle across the mouth before she could straighten.

Blood spread warm over her tongue. She swallowed reflexively, then wished she hadn’t. The taste lingered: salt and metal, thick at the back of her throat. When she drew breath, her split lip stung against her teeth.

Her left eyelid had swollen until she could see only a narrow strip beneath it. The right was puffing too, tender and heavy. She kept blinking, trying to clear a blur that wouldn’t clear.

Beyond her opponent’s shoulder, money changed hands.

Mara threw a right. Too wide, too slow. It passed through empty air and pulled her off balance. His answer caught her cheek and turned her whole body with it.

This time the wall didn’t save her.

One knee hit the pavement. Cold water soaked through her trousers. She planted a palm beside a crushed cigarette and stayed there, breathing through her open mouth.

“Stay down,” her corner man said now.

Across from her, the other fighter waited with his fists at his chest. He was breathing hard, but he was steady. Mara watched his shoes while the alley slowly stopped moving.

She had come here needing the purse.

She was beginning to understand she might leave needing help.

## Easy Fresh Tomato Salsa

**Makes:** About 2 cups  
**Time:** 15 minutes

### Ingredients
- 4 medium ripe tomatoes, diced
- ¼ medium white onion, finely diced
- 1 jalapeño, finely chopped (remove seeds and ribs for less heat)
- ¼ cup chopped fresh cilantro
- 1–2 tablespoons fresh lime juice
- ½ teaspoon salt, plus more to taste
- 1 small garlic clove, minced (optional)

### Instructions
1. Combine the tomatoes, onion, jalapeño, cilantro, and garlic in a bowl.

**Plato’s *The Republic*** is a philosophical dialogue, written around 375 BCE, in which Socrates and several companions explore a central question: **What is justice, and why should we be just?** Their inquiry leads to discussions of politics, education, knowledge, and the good life.

### Justice in the city and the individual
Socrates rejects the idea that justice is merely obeying rules or serving the interests of the powerful. To understand it, he proposes examining justice on a larger scale: an ideal city.

The city has three main groups:
- **Rulers**, who govern through wisdom.
- **Auxiliaries**, who defend the city and uphold its laws.
- **Producers**, who provide goods and services.

A city is just when each group performs its proper role in a harmonious whole. Socrates argues that the individual soul has a similar structure: **reason, spirit, and appetite**. A just person is one whose reason governs, whose spirit supports reason, and whose desires remain properly ordered. Justice is therefore an inner harmony, not simply outwardly good behavior.

### Philosopher-rulers and education
The ideal rulers are philosophers because they seek truth rather than wealth or power. Their education prepares them to understand the **Form of the Good**, the ultimate source of intelligibility and value.

Plato illustrates this education through the famous **Allegory of the Cave**: prisoners mistake shadows for reality until one escapes and discovers the world outside. The philosopher likewise moves beyond appearances toward genuine understanding—and must then return to help govern society.

The proposed city includes controversial measures, such as censorship of poetry and communal property and family arrangements for its guardians. It also allows women with the appropriate abilities to serve as guardians and rulers.

### Unjust societies and unhappy souls
Socrates describes a sequence of political decline: ideal rule gives way to **timocracy** (rule centered on honor), **oligarchy**, **democracy**, and finally **tyranny**. Each regime corresponds to a kind of character. The tyrant, seemingly the most powerful person, is actually enslaved by uncontrolled desires.

### Central conclusion
*The Republic* argues that **justice is worth pursuing for its own sake**: a well-ordered soul lives better than one dominated by greed, ambition, or fear. The closing **Myth of Er**, about judgment after death and the choice of future lives, reinforces the importance of choosing wisely and cultivating virtue.

If you mean a **flat tire on a car**, here’s how to change it safely.

### Before you start
- Pull onto **firm, level ground**, well away from traffic. Turn on your hazards, put the car in Park (or in gear for a manual), and set the parking brake.
- **If you’re on a narrow shoulder or near moving traffic, call roadside assistance rather than attempting the change.**
- Get the spare, jack, and lug wrench. Check your owner’s manual for the correct **jacking point** and any model-specific instructions.

### Change the tire
1. **Block the wheel diagonally opposite the flat** with wheel chocks to help prevent rolling.

One sunny afternoon, a mighty lion lay sleeping beneath a tree. A little mouse, hurrying through the grass, accidentally scampered across the lion’s nose.

The lion woke with a roar and trapped the mouse beneath his enormous paw.

“How dare you disturb my sleep!” he growled.

“Please let me go,” squeaked the mouse. “If you spare me, perhaps someday I can help you.”

The lion laughed. “A tiny creature like you help a lion like me?”

But the mouse looked so frightened that the lion lifted his paw. “Go on, then.”

“Thank you!” cried the mouse, and he hurried away.

A few days later, the lion was walking through the forest when he stepped into a hunter’s net. The ropes snapped tight around him. He struggled and roared, but the more he fought, the more tangled he became.

The little mouse heard the roaring and ran to find him.

“Hold still,” said the mouse. “I’ll help you!”

With his sharp teeth, he began gnawing at the ropes. He chewed through one, then another, until at last the net fell open and the lion stepped free.

“You were right,” said the lion, bowing his great head. “Even a little mouse can help a mighty lion.”

And from that day on, the lion never judged anyone’s worth by their size.

**Moral: No act of kindness is wasted, and even the smallest friend can make a big difference.**
